speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN-SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I beg to move the motion
of which I gave notice two or three days ago:
That, a special committee consisting of Messrs. Black (Halifax), Sir Henry Drayton, Duff, Sir Eugene Fiset, Halbert, Johnston, Kennedy (Glengarry), Leader, McKay, McMaster, McMurray, Rinfret, Sinclair (Queens), Stevens, and Stork be appointed to consider the resolution to give the government of Canada control over certain ocean rates by confirming an agreement between His Majesty and Sir William Petersen, K.C.B.E., as set out in said resolution with power to call for persons, papers and records, and to report from time to time.	*
Before submitting the resolution, Mr. Speaker, may I say that my attention has been drawn to the fact that some hon. members of the House feel that the resolution as drafted is not worded in a manner which would permit the committee to inquire into any other method that offers effective control of ocean rates. The government had assumed that it would be impossible to decide on one method without considering other methods as well and therefore that the resolution was sufficiently broad as it stood. However, to remove any possible doubt as to the scope which the committee will have I should like, with the permission of the House, to add after the words "set out in said resolution", "or by any other method that offers effective control".

subtopic: AGREEMENT WITH SIR WILLIAM PETERSEN-SPECIAL COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The addition of these words by the Prime Minister gives me an opportunity to speak to the resolution now before the House. I had intended if that opportunity did not come to me in this wray that I would try and get it by moving an amendment to the proposal as has been the practice hitherto in this House; and if hon. gentlemen will bear with me I will try to show-and I will not take very long-why the scope of the committee should be widened in the direction of getting greater control of ocean rates, and having other means suggested to
Ocean Shipping Rates

the committee than the means contained in the resolution. To bring that out I am going to take the liberty of presenting my views to the House on this occasion, and to shorten the time I propose to read, with the permission of hon. gentlemen, a few observations. I have taken some time in preparing these observations, and I hope the House will pardon me if I read them. I will be prepared at the conclusion to answer any questions that may be put to me by any hon. members. I begin to read:
At a previous stage of this debate, when the Minister of Trade and Commerce asked approval of the Petersen contract in the matter of ocean freights, I took occasion not only to dissent to that proposal but to suggest on my own responsibility what I thought was a much better plan of getting control of freight rates on the north Atlantic and a much better means of disciplining this north Atlantic combine.
My suggestion was for the Canadian government to take the necessary steps to secure the consolidation of the Canadian Pacific and all its steamship services with the Canadian National railways, which latter was in the control of the Canadian merchant marine, a consolidation which would secure enormous savings to the two railways, as well as give to the people and shippers of Canada improved transportation, not only on land but on the high seas and our other waterways.
The House heard me in silence, but two days later the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) rose in his place and did me the honour of saying that my plan was the most feasible scheme he had yet heard for dealing with this great problem of sea and land transportation. Some other hon. members spoke in the same strain, and on March 19, the Toronto Globe which is certainly more than friendly to the administration, had a leading article dealing with what they called my "bold proposal of the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National railways being consolidated into one system '' and quoted still further in the editorial from the speech of the member for North Waterloo, that I have just mentioned. It said that " Mr. Euler had declared that he had it on the highest authority that if the two systems could be combined a saving of from fifty millions to seventy-five millions a year could be effected," and I believe the hon. member for North Waterloo had good authority for that view. And then the Globe went on to say that if there could not be immediate consolidation of the two systems, there was no reason why some kind of pool as between the two could not be

effected, not only for their own benefit but for the benefit of Canada, and said further:
If amalgamation is regarded as impossible at present, why should there not be co-operation? Why should not the two systems pool their advantages for , their own benefit and that of Canada? Why not cease wasteful competition and useless duplication, and spend money on constructions only where it is needed for development? The interrats of the Canadian National Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway need not conflict. The bond of union between them is national service. They can prosper only as the country prospers and grows. A new era of prosperity for Canada might dawn if the two transcontinental systems were working heartily together for the common cause.
Sir Henry Thornton has made good. He has completely answered those who contended that a railway publicly owned and operated could not be managed as successfully as a private concern. The National Railway System can now stand comparison with its rival in every respect. Rivalry in service, so long as it is not merely for show and prestige, is healthy. Rivalry should not interfere with co-operation which might save money for both systems and for the country.
But this is not all of the approvals of my plan. While I spoke in silence in the House,
I knew that the members and country were with me both in scheme and in effect; and I continued to receive many words of approval in the lobbies and by mail and otherwise; and wdiat strengthened me most of all was a letter from a very close observer of public affairs in Canada, who said:
I should not be the least surprised if the future should vindicate your policy as to the fusion of the. Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific; I see many signs that the Canadian Pacific are getting very nervous over the competition which they are experiencing from the Canadian National: and I should think it quite possible that the time will come when they will demand that the government take them over.
And another witness appeared in this House last Thursday in favour of my proposal to consolidate the Canadian Pacific with the Canadian National, namely, the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), leader of the Progressives. In his speech on the budget, he brought up the question of the finances of the National Railways and advocated amongst other things the fixing of a fair amount as the capitalization of the Canadian National and then, passing on, he came to my suggestion of the merging of the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific systems; and while I take it that he declared himself in favour of some kind of working arrangement as between the two roads, the thing he had in his heart was the complete merging of the two and the immense saving that would accrue from such a consolidation. Hon. gentlemen who wish to know exactly what he did say will find it in Hansard, page 1581.
And now I want to quote another newspaper that, like the Toronto Globe and the

Ocean Shipping Rates
Winnipeg Free Press, believes in some kind of merger, and that is managed by a man veiy well known in this country and very well known in Montreal which city is supposed to be the home of the duplex system of railways; I refer to Mr. John R. Dougall who, in the Montreal Witness of the date of March 25, came out with this editorial:
Reductions of the cost of needless duplication of railway service seems to be looming up in the Commons as a live question. As the big railway batne usually conies during the sessions of the committee on National Railway estimates, much may be heard of this problem in a few weeks. Mr. Maclean, of Toronto, has won a new disciple in the person of Mr. Euler, for the cause of railway amalgamation. The latter is quite certain that sixty millions annually could be saved by this course. Other members from the west tell of train after train leaving Winnipeg with only thirty passengers aboard. In the provincial arena, Mr. Taschereau asks, " How long must the people pay the cost of running nine trains per day between Montreal and Quebec when three or four would do? " It will be remembered that Mr. Beatty, of the Canadian Pacific Railway, in a speech at Boston last fall mentioned consolidation as a possible solution of the problem. He emphatically added, however, that he did not believe the country would consider this procedure at present. He is in an excellent position to know. But if there is no general approval of either consolidation under public or private ownership there most certainly is a demand for immediate elimination of expensive and needless duplication of service. Few are so blind or so thoughtless as to fail to see that, regardless of who owns the lines, the country pays for all extravagance in the end. Canada has faith in the efficiency of the Canadian Pacific. There is now confidence that the National management is determinedly meeting a difficult situation. For these reasons there is all the more reason to expect that the heads of the systems can get together and agree on a programme of drastic curtailment of needless extravagance, which neither road could make singly without losing business to its rival, but which if effected would benefit both as well as the country in general.
And if I must quote another witness, I am going to put E. W. Beatty, president of 'the Canadian Pacific, on the stand. He spoke of economy in Canadian public affairs; and in an interview given out at Toronto be is thus reported:
If business principles prevailed, the national policy would be to render the discharge of all our obligations that are proper and possible, with due recognition of the necessity of the individual and corporate thrift.
Now these last words about "corporate thrift," if I may interpret them, ought to mean thrift on the part of the Canadian Pacific Railway, so as to fit in with the situation which confronts us, namely, the inability of this country to maintain two great transcontinental roads working in every province of Canada, in a condition of expensive, heedless and altogether unnecessary rivalry, when one system would be much better and would save the country seventy million dollars a
year. This is not the day for duplex railways.
And while I criticize Mr. Beatty, I admit his outstanding ability, and that as a railway executive he is the equal of anyone on the continent; and, furthermore, he is a graduate of my own university and won his spurs by his own abilities; and I admit he 'believes in mergers; but he wants to be the one who does the merging and the one who takes the hand of the lady; while my view of it is that the Canadian National, Which is absolutely a Canadian enterprise, should merge the Canadian Pacific, and that the Princess Eddy should gladly offer her hand to Sir Henry. And, speaking of Mr. Beatty in the personal sense, I can compliment him, if I may, by saying that his eyebrows are almost as pronounced as my own. He, too, may have "big eyes" as others have said of myself.

speechtext:
With all due respect to your correction, Sir, I stand by that. 1 will soon make the connection, but I want to come to it in such a way that the public as well as this House can appreciate it.
As for the Canadian Pacific itself, I have always been favourable to that railway, and, as a member of this House, and before I was a member of this House, I knew its chief promoters, Lord Mount Stephen, Lord Strathcona, Sir William Van Horne, Lord Shaughnessy, when they were ordinary men without title, but when they had the ability, the foresight, or shall I say the vision, to plan that great road and to make a splendid success of it, and it is with us to-day.
Ocean Shipping Rates

But the transportation problem now before Canada and before this House is bigger than the Canadian Pacific, and all I say is that it would be to the interest of the country, and I think, the interest of the shareholders of that company, that a merger of all the services of the Canadian Pacific with the Canadian National should take place to-day before there is more raiding of a good Canadian security on the New York stock exchange. The main weakness of the Canadian Pacific is that its stock to-day is owned outside of Canada, and kicked about the New York and London stock markets whenever they like, and the control thereof might pass any day into the hands of an American railway. The Canadian National is absolutely owned by the people of Canada; it is subject to our policy and our policy as a nation only, and finally we cannot keep up a duplex system of railways, one-half of which might be held in Canada and the other half outside of Canada.
But, as I said, you will not find in Canadian papers now anything about things like these that are going on in the United States. You will hardly find one telling in its financial columns what has really been going on in the New York stock exchange more or less for a month back, and that is that the great railroads of the United States, including the Union Pacific, the Northern Pacific, the New York Central and the Canadian Pacific, have had a significant fall in prices. The Canadian Pacific has probably dropped ten points within almost the same number of days; other American roads have 'come down much lower, and apparently the end has not been reached. So, I ask this House and the country why the newspapers of Canada do not tell of things going on in New York in regard to railway shares and mergers of the railways of America and Canada.
When I am speaking of the newspapers of this country and this proposal for the merging of the two great railways into one, I am reminded of the fact that we now have in Canada what are called "chain groceries." Extending that idea, I say there are some people who think we have chain newspapers in this country and that they are pretty well "chained" at the present time. They say even that one man sitting in a big job-printing establishment in Montreal, doing the printing for both the railways and some other big interests in this country, after he is through with the job-printing propositions before him, also undertakes to operate a chain of newspapers from the Atlantic to the Pacific with a duplex line of editorials to suit the circum-

stances of the locality in which the appeal is made. Great is the duplex idea in Montreal, as to railways, as to press, and as to sports and sport clothes for .men and women. Public economies do not count these days.
Now I want to come to the question of mergers of railways and to deal with the innuendo that I am proposing something new. I want to tell the House and the country that the consolidation and merging of the railways of the United States is the most pressing question there to-day; that it is the fixed policy of the Coolidge administration, as it was the fixed policy of the McKinley administration and even of the Wilson administration, to wipe out hundreds of the smaller lines of the United States and to merge them at the most into eight regional organizations, some of them covering more than six or eight states of the union, in one consolidated system. This work has been going on for years and1 is pretty nearly completed. The duty has been imposed upon the Interstate Commerce Commission to effect these consolidations and they are at the work now every day. One of these consolidations is that of the Nickelplate with the Chesapeake and Ohio, which is now not only before the courts for decision, but also before the Interstate commission. But that is not all. As a matter of fact, the New York Central has completed its proposed regional system, so has the Pennsylvania, and in the New York World of March 26 there is a special from Washington which says:
Special dispatch to the World, Washington, March 25. Comprehensive railway legislation-the most far-reaching undertaken since the passage of the Esch-Cummins Transportation Act-will be begun at the opening of the next session of Congress, leaders on both sides of the Capitol admitted to-day.
Senator A. B. Cummins, author of the present act, already has a bill prepared calling for compulsory consolidation of the roads into a series of major Streams, while the House committee on Interstate Commerce will start hearings early in September to prepare a bill for presentation to Congress as soon as it convenes.
The tax reduction bill and farm relief legislation will be submitted at the same time, confronting the administration with its three most difficult and embarrassing problems the moment Congress assembles.
Besides compulsory consolidation, other railroad questions are the completion of valuation of the roads and a determination as to what will be done with the huge fund now building up and available to the government under the recapture clause to bolster up weaker roads with loans.
A tentative system of consolidations was worked out by the Interstate Commerce Commission, but railroads which object to being hitched up with weaker lines have made the tentative plan abortive. Whether the administration will approve any plan designed to compel the railroads to amalgamate has not been made known.

Ocean Shipping Rates
And in its leading editorial of the same day, the New York World criticizes the Nickel-plate consolidation; its opening sentence is: Congress has approved the policy of railroad consolidation by voluntary agreement and before long a plan for the first of the great consolidations will be submitted to the Interstate Commerce Commission for its approval. It is being promoted by the Van Sweringen brothers of Cleveland. They propose to put together the old Nickel Plate, the Erie, the Pere Marquette, the Hocking Valley and the Chesapeake and Ohio.
On the general theory that consolidation of strong and weak roads is desirable there is now general agreement; there is, in fact, strong opinion in favour of making consolidation compulsory. It is all the more important, then, that the first practical test of the policy should be above serious criticism.
And the last sentence reads as follows:
The Van Sweringen merger needs looking into, not only as a matter of justice to the Chesapeake and Ohio stock holders, but also because it is important to establish sound methods at the beginning of this era of railroad consolidations. Anything like a scandal in this, the first great merger, would disgust the public with the policy of mergers and would deeply injure the railroads as a whole.
From now on mergers either voluntary or forced will be the big question in railroad America and railroad Canada.
Now, I want to come to my proposals. I have re-written this very carefully, andi it is what I desire to present to the House and the country in dealing with this merging of railways so as to reach a solution of the question of regulation of ocean freight rates. This is my proposal in a word:
Proposed consolidation of the Canadian Pacific and subsidiaries with the Canadian National, involving:
1.	Such re-routing of main lines and1 branches as might be dictated by the better grades, mountain passes, bridge-crossings, tunnels, approaches to stations, etc., held by one or other of the companies;
2.	The consolidation of the cartage, telegraph and express services of the systems,-perhaps taking over the parcel post, postal and money orders of the post office,-thereby cutting out all unnecessary services and buildings, rents, etc., and perhaps using local post offices at places as aids to these national services;
3.	The cutting out of all unnecessary trackage, bridges, tunnels, stations, buildings, tanks, plants, etc., and thereby releasing material for any double trackage required, or other additions that the traffic thus re-routed and consolidated might call for;
4.	Also cutting out all unnecessary executives and staffs, officials and offices, headquarters, and attendant expenses;
5.	Also cutting out and selling any unnecessary engines and unnecessary official sleeping, dining, passenger, postal, freight and

With all due deference
to the hon. member, I fear he is not discussing the point. I have too much respect for the hon. gentleman to lecture him, but I do think he might come to the point; I am waiting in expectation that he will reach it.

I am sure Mr. Speaker's hopes will be realized. Further, there would be involved the general bringing about of greater efficiency, better service, lower freights and fares, increased economy, ending forever all extravagant and unprofitable rivalry.
The Canadian Pacific has been generously treated by the Canadian people and parliament in the way of legislation, charters, plans, surveys, monej'' subsidies, land grants, rights of way, exemptions of many kinds and protection by a fair and just railway commission maintained at the public expense; yet this great beneficiary and ward of the nation, notwithstanding its enterprise and devotion to the work and service called for in its franchises and contracts, has at times shown a spirit of ingratitude and at other times developed an attitude that the Canadian Pacific was more than the nation and parliament which had created it; and that it even now enjoys or thinks it enjoys a free hand to crush out or interfere with any right of the nation to engage in public ownership in the way of transportation and other services; in a word, that the created company is greater than its creator and benefactor, the nation. This public servant must not set up to be the master rather than the servant of parliament and the people; each must be fair to the other.'
The Canadian Pacific can claim to have made a success of its railways and other services and is entitled to full recognition therefor; but, on its part, this great company must
Ocean Shipping Rates

recognize that besides all the successive aids and grants to it from the country, it has from the very first secured for its chief promoters and owners of its shares, peerages, baronetcies, knighthoods and other honours, fortunes for themselves and friends; and that the country was equally generous to the promoters and bankers of rival railway lines that ultimately became bankrupt; and that these later promoters and bankers also shared in the baronetcies and other honours and profits and appointments of various kinds and had all their company debts taken over and paid by an overtasked and overtaxed public.
Notwithstanding all which the public and the people found and are finding most of the money-outside of the Canadian Pacific's shares and bond issues-and all the traffic for these railways, at high rates; and therefore, in a word, that company must listen to a public demand for consolidation and unified operating costs when it comes up as it does come up to-day in this House and in the country; and the public likewise must be fair in the matter of compensation to the hitherto successful Canadian Pacific.
The Chicago, Milwaukee and St. Paul and many other railways now under fire on the New York Stock Exchange are a warning even to the successful Canadian Pacific. Great moneymaking propositions and successful services are ever threatened by scrapping. All transportation is being scrapped to-day. The automobile, the autobus, the motor truck are taking the local passenger, freight, cartage and express business from the big railways; and the aeroplane will soon reach for the long distance travel, mail and express business; the sleeping and dining car business is in danger, even a lot of the hotel patronage is threatened when business men and others come to know that interview's over wire or wireless are as efficient as personal visits involving long jumps by rail or road and the accompanying inconveniences. The new world may take a lot of the present rush out of business, and sanity take its place-overstraining may be at its peak.
There may be a wise time to sell a successful private-owned railway property, especially if in the near future the traffic were limited to long hauls of freight by land and sea; and if the Canadian Pacific should determine to sell, a commission of three men made up of the presidents of the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National and one other arbitrator ought to be able to fix a fair amount for the consideration of parliament as compensation to the Canadian Pacific shareholders for the transfer of all their services and assets to the 
National Railways. And such a consolidation of these roads and services might suggest to parliament the creation of a new corporation to be called National Canadian Carriers, an organization that would include these railway, ocean, express and telegraph services and other services on highways and waterways, said carriers being further empowered to take up, as need may call for, any coming developments in such service and communications of all kinds by radio, beam, wireless or cable, as inventors or promoters may be prepared to submit or the policy of the new consolidated directorate might determine or parliament order. All such common carriers in the widest sense to be national or under national control and in no way dictators to parliament or the nation. This is where the tragedy that is now at our doors will end and national prosperity begin afresh.
This programme of mine is, I hope, plain to all, and I ask hon. members to read it and I ask the country to read it. The outstanding deduction from it all is that Canada under her present financial strain cannot afford to maintain these two competing railways and other services, when one joint management and ownership would) give a much better and more economical service. Is it not absurd, for instance, that there should be two enormous headquarter buildings and headquarter staffs in the city of Montreal, one for the Canadian Pacific and another for the Canadian National, when one building would house both, when one set of officials could administer both systems and do it much better and for less money. Of all the pieces of extravagance before the world to-day, this is one that ought first to be put an end to and reason and economy govern in its place. It is not only an extravagance, it is a crime and there is not a member in this House that does not admit I am right, that does not think it should end now and forever.
Now as to how this consolidation could be effected, I have already hinted at it in my previous speech that it could be achieved in a very short time and that the economies effected would permit not only reduced freights by land and water but would bring about other economies in the telegraph, express and postal branches and that the whole of the financial commitments of the two systems could be met by these consequent savings and by re-arrangement of the securities involved. Members may laugh at the extent of the proposal and the commitments of it; but because it is large and because it is sweeping, it may justify itself. The real enormity is in the existence of two unneces-

Ocean Shipping Rates
sary systems at great cost when one would do much better and give immediate relief to all interested in transportation and communications.
I do not propose a single thing that is not what might be called an investment proposition; and I challenge the best financial authorities in this country or out of it to deny the conclusion which I have reached in favour of the consolidation. All our railway proposals were for the expenditure of further money of the taxpayers of Canada. For the first time I am proposing something that would at once lessen the burden of the Canadian taxpayers; and I want to say, that the First Minister has himself declared in this House that he has already approached the Canadian Pacific-to what extent I cannot at present say-but what he said is most significant, and what the Globe says for itself and its party is also significant, and what the others that I have quoted have said is also significant. Canada is at a crisis to-day. What it wants is courage in the government and in this parliament to deal with that crisis and by a new departure start our country and our people again on the up grade. Desperate conditions call for radical use of the knife and the stern orders of the dictator of retrenchment in times of the wildest extravagance. If the cure doesn't come a new Cromwell will; and even now you can almost hear his horses champing in their stalls, and later on in the lower corridors of this House.
And, finally, let me say to the House and to this parliament in the. matter of duplex services: Coming in at our centre door, under the tower, what do I see? Duplex post offices double-manned with two postmasters and two deputy postmasters-one set for the Commons and one set for the Senate-and double sorters in the two offices; also a duplex system of accountancy and a battery of clerks as timekeepers on members and senators, and a double staff of writers of indemnity checks for the two houses; also duplicate barber shops; duplicate Hansard staffs; duplicate messenger staffs-

Order. The hon. member's remarks with respect to two railway systems and ocean rates were in order, but when he begins to discuss the internal organization of the House of Commons and the Senate he is absolutely out of order.

I bow to your ruling, Mr. Speaker. I was amply trying to show that this extravagance which is common to transportation also prevails in other quarters, and if we start to cure it in our 109i
own House we will the sooner cure the duplication in connection with our railways and our ocean services. That completes my argument anyway, Mr. Speaker. My .point is that you cannot deal effectively with ocean rates by establishing such a one-horse system as the government now propose. But if we have the enterprise to take over the Canadian Pacific Railway and its steamship service-and it is one of the best in the world-and merge them with the National Railways and our merchant marine, we shall at once secure absolute control of land and ocean rates. This consolidation would effect very great economy of operation-upwards of $70,000,000 a year- and would give us an ocean service under our absolute control. If the government want to arrive at a real settlement of the problem they must do something along these lines. Then Canada will publicly own all her transportation facilities, and so give 'the people service at cost. We dh not want to have anything to do with the north Atlantic conference or combine. I admit that it is one of the worst combines in the world, that it is trying to fleece the people of Canada-everyone admits that now-and that it should be disciplined. My argument, Mr. Speaker, is that the only way to discipline this combine is by consolidating our two railway systems and their steamship services into one transportation system under one national management, absolutely owned1 by the people of the Dominion. Once you have done that you will be able to say for the first time to those whom you invite to settle our vacant lands: "We invite you to a country of hope, to a country where you will have the cheapest transportation by land or sea for the products of your farms and of your factories." I hope the government will accept my suggestion. I also hope that they will widen the scope of the committee and allow anybody to appear before it, I am going to appear before that committee and express my views in a much more pronounced form than I have to-day. I hope my friend down the line, the leader of the Progressives (Mr. Forke) will also go there with his representations.
I believe that the people of Canada to-day are determined to finish for all time extravagant expenditure wherever it appears, especially in connection with transportation. While I was quite properly called to order by you, Mr. Speaker, when I pointed out the duplication of workers right in these houses of parliament, I only pointed out that what has taken place in connection with transportation in this country, has also occurred
Ocean Shipping Rates

Mr. Speaker, before we proceed further with this motion I would call the attention of the House to the composition of the proposed committee. It is to be composed of eight Liberals^ four Progressives and three Conservatives. Why is it that the Progressive party with practically the same membership as the Conservative party is allowed one more member on the committee? I would remind the House that there are thirteen members in this part of the chamber who do not pay allegiance to the Progressive party, and they have no representation on the committee. Under the circumstances I presume that the Progressive party is to be represented by four members because of the fact that the thirteen members to whom I have referred are included in the party.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I would suggest to the Prime Minister that in order to give all the elements in this House proper representation on the committee he should1 increase its membership by two or three at least, because it is not fair that our thirteen members should have no representation on a committee of such importance. Some few days ago there appeared in the press an announcement that there had been born in this House a new political party. I contradict that statement emphatically. We thirteen members who do not belong to any of the three major parties in this House met together for the purpose of seeing to it that we got proper representation on any special committees that might be appointed from time to time. That is all we met for; consequently I wish to deny the suggestion that a new party has been born in this House. I would request the Prime Minister to take into consideration the representations that I have made in this regard

and try to provide representation on this committee for these thirteen members.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: With respect to the constitution of the committee the government has followed the usual procedure. As to increasing the number on the committee, the unanimous consent of the House is required; but if that is the ivish of the House the government does not mind if the committee is made larger. But as to the personnel, I simply wish to point out that the government is following the practice that was adopted when this parliament came into being and that was followed at the beginning of this session in striking the general committees of the House. Unless some substantial reason to the contrary can be offered, I question very much whether at this stage in the life of the present parliament it would be wise to depart from that practice.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot see how the contention advanced by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gardiner) can be logically disputed. Nor does it seem necessary that the committee be enlarged in order to meet it. The committee has fifteen members now. Eight are from the government side, four from the fifty hon. members to my left and three from the fifty-one hon. members here. It is not my intention to dwell very long on this matter of protection. I have said in this House before, and I re-state at this time, that in my opinion protection breeds trusts and tends to distrust in government. We heard from the hon. member for Dufferin (Mr. Woods) a short time ago in regard to the manufacture of wire fencing in this country, and I think it is worth while repeating some of his statements. We have different firms manufacturing wire fencing in Canada. Some of them, also manufacture the wire or raw steel rods. In this particular instance the manufacturers who weave wire fencing also manufacture a fencing of No. 10 wire, on which there is an import duty of 20 per cent. These other people who only weave wire are forced to pay that 20 per cent duty to their competitors, with the result that they will either be put out of business or we will have another trust in this country. My hon. friend at that time spoke about manufacturing in the small towns of Ontario years ago. I remember very well as a boy in this country, that in the town where I was brought up we had many small manufacturing establishments. We had a foundry employing fifteen or twenty men, a tannery employing about an equal number, and a woollen mill, three different firms that manufactured wagons, sleighs, buggies and so on, but all these had disappeared, before 1896. And why? Probably because something similar to what I have stated in connection with the wire 
fencing obtained-that the big fellow was able to freeze them out. I think it can be safely said that protection has failed to make Canada prosperous. I do not wish to burden the House with a long array of figures to sustain this statement I have made as to the failure of protection to make Canada prosperous, but there are a few to which I should like to call attention. Take for example the comparison between the growth of Canada and the United States during comparable periods in their early development. In 1790, the United States had a population of 3,929,000, which compares with 3,689,000 for Canada at the time of confederation. In the first fifty years after 1790 the population of the United States rose to 17,063,000; while in the first fifty years of its history the population of this Dominion only reached 8,361,000. I have taken the United States figures from the Encyclopedia Britan-nica and the Canadian from the Year Book. In the first fifty years of its existence, or thereabout, the United States increased in population more than four-fold, while the population of Canada during a similar period was only a little more than doubled. This does not look as if Canada had in the last forty odd years enjoyed, under protection, the growth that it was entitled to in the normal course of events.
Or, if more evidence is desired of the ineffectiveness of protection as a national policy -that is a policy that will build up Canada- we have only to look at the figures of emigration to the United States, which our Conservative friends have been so fond of citing of late. I do not need to quote them here, for they have been brought before us quite lately by the right hon. member -who leads the official opposition (Mr. Meighen). Any one who is curious can find the figures up to recent years in The Monthly Labour Review, published by the United States Department of Labour, -which showed an annual exodus of 117,000 in the United States fiscal year 1922-23.
Instead of quoting these figures of the United States government, however, I prefer to cite a table from the last issue of the Canada Year Book 1922-23, page 149. In that table the Bureau of Statistics reviews the movement of Canada's population in the last two decades-1901 to 1911 and 1911 to 1921. In the first of these decades the numbers added to the population of this country by natural increase and by immigration were 2,701,217; while the actual increase in the population was only 1,835,328. In the second decade the numbers added by immigration

The Budget-Mr. Johnston
and by birth were 2,879,580; while the actual increase in the population was only 1,581,840. In other words in the first of these decades, one of the most prosperous in the history of Canada, and under a fu|ly developed protective policy, there was an exodus from the country of 865,000 and in the second ten year period the loss of population was 1,297,000. Surely the existence of such figures as these after thirty or forty years of protection is evidence that there is something wrong in that " heaven-born " system as a national policy. And I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that the figures pertaining to the last decade I have mentioned cannot bring much comfort to my hon. friends to my right, because it was they who were in office from 1911 to 1921, under a highly protective system, under which Canada has lost so many people to the United States.

speechtext:
Yes; these are for the
year 1924 when the Crowsnest rates on wheat and wheat products were in full force. I would read now the following press despatch;
Would be Canada's Richest Men To-day E. W. Beatty Says Canadian Northern Builders Should Have Served Prairies Alone
New York, February 22.-Over sixteen hundred members of the New York Traffic Club, and the largest gathering in the history of the organization, were present at the annual banquet in the Commodore Hotel here last night, where E. W. Beatty, K.C., president and chairman of the Canadian Pacific Railway, was the chief speaker. The guests included the executives of many of the larger United States railroads. W. A. Schumacher, president of the Club, was in the chair.
Mr. Beatty was accompanied by W. R. Mclnnes, of the C.P.R. Mr. Beatty largely devoted his remarks to a review of Canada's railway history, which was, he said, the story of the great achievement, mistakes, failures and political and economic complications ending with the most unique situation existing in the world to-day. He traced the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and said that the success of the company had provoked similar but over-ambitious enterprises. He referred to the Canadian Northern which, he said, while a great conception, carried to physical completion, had failed because it was built before its time and could not be operated successfully through the dislocation of war time.
"If," said the speaker,-
And I would draw the attention of the House to this.
"If", said the speaker, "instead of turning its prairie lines into a portion of a transcontinental system the owners had been content to make as their termini the mountains on the west, and the Great Lakes on the [DOT] east, they would have been the wealthiest men in Canada".
There is only one inference to be drawn from the foregoing and it is, that the handling of grain in the prairies to-day is the most lucrative traffic in which the railway companies are engaged.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the
House rose at six o'clock I was discussing transportation rates in Canada, (particularly railway rates. I also mentioned lake and ocean rates. As the latter subject is coming before a special committee of the House of which I am a member, I shall refrain from discussing it now. With respect to lake rates, in my opinion, judging from the information I have, the producers of wheat in western Canada have been harder hit by the
exorbitant tolls levied by the lake carriers than they have been by ocean rates. In this connection I think it is not too much to say that when the rush of grain is on, and the rate to Buffalo is one-half cent lower than the rate to lake ports, our coastal laws should be suspended.
Now I come to a matter which probably is somewhat irrelevant to the motion before the House; nevertheless, I think it is of sufficient interest to occupy the attention of hon. members for a short time. I refer to the appointment by this House last session of three commissioners to visit the Wembley exhibition. I happened to be one of those commissioners, and as there has been some criticism of the vote, I wish to state my position in regard to it and to justify the expenditure. The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) told us the other day that he had discussed this vote on the stump, and when he discussed it in the House he said that the cost of the commission was covered by a vote of $20,000. He would have been more fair had he said the cost was smothered by a vote of S20.000, for the total cost of the commission was $4,200, or $1,400 for each of the three commissioners. It is not my intention to try to justify the vote upon its smallness; if it will not stand on principle, it will not stand at all; but when we take into consideration that this House voted over a million dollars to place Canada's products on exhibition at Wembley, I think there was some justification for sending a small delegation from parliament in order that they might bring back a report.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Particularly as all the members were also Canadian products.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Our report is now in
the hands of the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Robb), and a perusal of it will show that it contains a recommendation that Canada should participate in the exhibition for 1925. Whether our recommendation had anything to do with the government's decision I do not know, but I am glad that they have decided that Canada shall again take part in the exhibition this year. I do not intend to deal with the matter in detail on this occasion; my remarks in that connection will be more appropriate when the minister's estimates are before the House; but it may be of interest to hon. members to know that all men of affairs in this country did not support the official opposition in their stand against the vote in question. I have in my hand a letter from a well known figure in Canada, and I will read that part of it which applies to the matter I am discussing:
The Budget-Mr. Johnston

J. Fred Johnston, M.P.,
Bladworth, Sask.
Dear Mr. Johnston,
May I congratulate you on the substance of the interview you gave the Saskatoon Star and which appeared September 24th, on your visit to Wembley? I have just drawn the attention of my different editors to some phases of the interview and have sent the article as a whole to the editor of The Financial Post, suggesting that he reproduce it in next week's issue.
We supported the govement in the expenditure on the exhibition, believing in it just as you do; and we also supported the action of the government in giving a grant for M.P's to go abroad. We believed that both appropriations were very good investments.
Faithfully yours,
J. B. Maclean.
Mr. Maclean, is publisher of Maclean's Magazine.
Those of us who did go to Wembley were very sorry indeed that the chief whip of the Conservative party (Mr. Boys) was unable to go. The House knows that he supported the vote and was anxious to go, but for personal reasons be could mot get away. I hope the government will see its way clear to let the hon. member go this year; and I think he should be accompanied by one or two other members of this House. I believe they could do good work for Canada by visiting the Wembley exhibition. It was our privilege the second day, I think, after we arrived at Wembley to welcome to the Canadian building 'Certain members of the Imperial government, and the occasion was a source of great satisfaction to us.
From the opening of the exhibition in April until the time we left, an average of twenty thousand school children a day passed through the turnstiles to visit the exhibition. These children were alii at the age when their minds were most receptive, and they could not but be impressed by the splendid exhibit of our products in the Canada building. I feel confident, Mr. Speaker, that if the government or the House would accept some of the proposals and 'recommendations contained in the report of the commissioners the cost of sending them to Wembley would be returned to this country many times.
A particular phase of the matter that I wish to emphasize is the effectiveness of the manner in which Canada was placed before the Britisher who travels abroad. It was my pleasure to meet many who intended to visit Canada. One trip through the Canada building could not but create a desire to see the real thing, and I am informed by the officials who were in charge of this end of the work at Wembley that long before the exhibition closed last Ml many travelers from England were touring our country. I do think we

give too little attention to this matter of tourist travel. It is estimated that last year the revenue coming to Canada from tourist travel was over $136,000,000, and the only money we spend in a direct way to induce tourist travel is a vote of $35,000. Of this amount $12,000 is used for salaries, 'leaving $23,000 for what may be termed propaganda. I have made the assertion, and I stand by it, that the total cost of Canada's exhibit at Wembley will be returned to this country, not by ordinary tourist travel but by increased tourist .travel in a very Hiort time. Other countries are paying a great deal of attention to the matter. In 1919, I think it was, France created a department of government under a minister whose business it was to look after tourist travel in that country. We know what Italy and Switzerland do in this connection; they almost live on the revenues derived in their respective countries from this source. I will try to give to the House some idea of the benefit that is bound to come to Canada and what we may expect if we extend our energies a little. I think they are more alive to this question out on 'the west coast than here in the eastern parts of our Dominion. Vancouver has a publicity commissioner who gives a great deal of time to this matter, and here is something he says:
According to estimates carefully worked out by Mr. Davison, Publicity Commissioner for Vancouver, approximately one-third of every dollar left in the country by tourists finds its way back into the pockets of the rural districts. In the year 1924 it is estimated that one million tourists visited British Columbia. According to Commissioner Davison these visitors consumed-
I am not going to give the total in pounds, but it is remarkable. What I want to get at is how this money is distributed and who gets the benefits. Canadian food products consumed amount to $30,000,000; foreign, $14,000,000. The other $92,000,000 is made up in this way: transportation, railways, steamships, $28,-000,000-that is where our National railways come in; hotel accommodation, personal services, $56,000,000; equipment, clothing and so forth, $3,500,000; amusements, souvenirs and so forth, $3,500,000; miscellaneous, $1,000,000, making $92,000,000. This, added to the food consumed, $44,000,000, makes a total of $136,000,000 as the estimated revenue coming to Canada last year. As I have pointed out, all we are spending in this connection is, at the most, $35,000. It goes without saying that in no other activity do we get a like revenue for such a comparatively small expenditure. There are some things which are necessary if we are to increase tourist traffic in this

The Budget-Mr. Johnston
country. We are pretty well equipped so far as railways are concerned, but we must have motor highways. I was pleased that the Minister of Railways moved to amend the Highways Act of 1919 by giving further time for the provinces to earn their grants under that statute and I hope that another year he will see his way to further supplement the vote for this purpose. Tourist travel comes to our country largely in motor cars from the south and if we have trunk roads, particularly in western Canada, to connect with the state roads we will take many thousands of people into the mountain sections that we would not get otherwise. I have here a comparative statement which should be of some interest to the House. If we were to compare the value of our four highest exports during the fiscal year 1921-22 with what I might call our "export of scenery" they would be seen to rank as follows: Agriculture and vegetables, $317,000,000; wood and paper, $179,000,000; animal products, $135,000,000; foreign tourist travel, $100,000,000; iron and its products, $27,000,000. That means that the "export of scenery" comes fourth in the list, and in selling our scenery to tourists all they take away with them is an eye-full and the food they consume, we have the scenery left to sell over again. I feel that there is a wonderful field for increasing this traffic in the Old Country, and I would suggest to the government that they send to Wembley this year the same man who was there last year. He is an expert photographer, and an expert also in handling moving pictures. Last year he went out into the country week ends and displayed his pictures, and the number of visitors he had in his office at the Wembley exhibition was remarkable. The cost of doing this is very slight if we compare it with many of our other activities, and it involves no new scheme of taxation:	It is simply a
matter of spending a little money in a direct way to induce more people to visit our country.
I am not going to detain the House much longer except to deal with this further point: We hear to-day rumours of an election, and one wonders what the issues are going to be. We heard the hon. member for Dufferin (Mr. Woods) say the other evening that back in 1911 he was in the councils of the Conservative party when it was decided they could not defeat the government of the day by attacking their policy but their only chance was by raising the loyalty cry or starting a flag waving exhibition, and they did not hesitate to do so. Now, I was rather amused on taking up the morning Citizen
of March 27 to read this from a speech by the right hon. leader of the opposition to west-end Conservatives:
If this country wishes to maintain British citizenship on the North American continent, it must turn right about from the way in which it is being led by the Mackenzie King administration.
I was just wondering whether that was the beginning of the Conservative campaign for next election. But horn, gentlemen to my right will find1 a vast difference in public opinion in this country from what obtained formerly. We had the remarks of the hon. member for Dufferin who at that time was attached to the party of whom I have just spoken, and a few weeks ago we had the words of the member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) with respect to the reciprocity pact. The House will remember that he said at that time that he was sorry he had voted against reciprocity in 1911, and hoped that he would get the opportunity to vote for a similar pact at an early date. There you have an expression of opinion from Ontario and another from Manitoba. I do not believe the Progressive party is going out of existence at the next election. It received support in 1921 from many of those who opposed the reciprocity pact in 1911, and who have seen the light. My Conservative friends will have a much harder task in winning public support for their policies than they had in 1911. I have here another reason why western Canada would not give much support to the Conservative party. Here is a Canadian press despatch from Halifax dated September 3:
Meighen Not in Sympathy With Prairie Provinces
Halifax, N.S., Sept. 3.-Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, speaking here Tuesday on the rapidly growing movement of the various provinces of Canada to secure better treatment under the confederation agreement, declared that while Canada was a "hard country to govern" the various problems would largely be solved if a more human touch was established with the extremities of the country.
The ex-premier said the prairie provinces think they are the only ones who have been denied the rights of the confederation pact.
"I am going to tell them," he said, "that I am not in sympathy with their grievances."
Now what are their problems and their grievances? We remember very well the attitude of the right hon. gentleman in 1922 when we were striving to get the Crowsnest pass rates re-established on wheat and wheat products in that western country. Both he and his party opposed us as vigorously as they could. If that is one of the grievances he is going to tell western Canada he does not sympathize with we already have that information. With respect to tariff matters

The Budget-Miss Macphail
neither the right hon. gentleman nor any person else need expect to make any headway in western Canada on a protectionist platform.
In conclusion let me say this:	I believe
there is a tendency in this country on the part of many people to look for governments to do for them that which they might better do for themselves. Personally I am opposed to what might be termed paternal legislation. Canada's problems to-day are not those of production. We can produce, and as a matter of fact are producing, more per capita than any other people in the world. That is established b3^ facts. Our problems are rather those of distribution and markets. In connection with these the government certainly has a responsibility, a big responsibility, and I hope it will address itself to their solution not only with vigour but with determination.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey):	Mr. Speaker, I wish at the very
beginning of my remarks to offer my congratulations to the hon. the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) on this his sixty-^sixth birthday. I think I am not going outside the bounds of truth when I say that I believe he is the most loved member in this whole chamber, loved not only by me but by all hon. members. It is something to be able to control or lure to oneself affection and regard as the Minister of Railways and Canals is able to do. It is possibly after all a greater success than any other kind of success that could come to one.
I am going to deal with a particular question, namely the condition that we now find in the area of the colliery towns of Cape Breton. I remember when I came to this House four years ago one of the first debates-at least the one which stays in my mind most vividly -was the one precipitated by, I think, the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) on a motion to adjourn the House to debate an urgent matter, which was then the proposal of the company to cut the men's wages thirty-seven and a half per cent, as I recollect, and a delegation came from Cape Breton asking that a royal commission be appointed to look into the matter. The British Empire Steel Corporation-shortly called "Besco"-is, as everyone in this House knows, a huge merger that absorbed twenty-four companies with a capital of eighty-three million dollars. They went into the merger that way, and as one company came out with a hundred and two million dollars of capital. This company is a very excellent example of pampering. They have received almost everything-subsidy, bonuses, protection by tariff

and militia. They have had almost everything any government could give them. I think when I am through hon. members will conclude with me-at least if they believe anything I say-that 'it is an excellent example of the pampering of industry and the neglect of humanity.
I wondered before I went to Glace Bay and the towns in the vicinity of Glace Bay where the strike occurred, at mines Nos. 2, 4 and 6, how it was that people, after just three weeks of unemployment, found themselves at once on the hunger line, and almost in fact unclothed; that is unclothed when one thinks of the cold wind. I wondered how that could occur in three weeks' time. I had of course an idea that surely it could not be just the result of three weeks of not working, and I find-and my visit confirmed me in this-that the condition now existing is an accumulation, and that the cessation of work three weeks ago has merely brought the matter to a head. For four years the men have not had regular work. For a year and a half they have had almost no work. In the Dominion mines Nos. 2, 4 and 6, affecting 2,200 men, 85 per cent of whom are Canadians, and many of the younger men of whom are veterans and returned soldiers, the men worked seven days in December, six days in January and four days in February. One man said to me, "Oh we make big pay when we work". But work is the difficult thing! They get fairly good pay all right, but they were not getting much work and by the time everything was checked off that had to be checked off their pay envelopes there was almost nothing left. One woman expressed it in this way to me, "For a year and a half we have just had enough to eat. We have let the stores of furniture, of bedding and household necessities go down. We have just been getting enough to eat." So that, when the credit given by the company's stores was cut off a little over three weeks ago and they ceased work, they not only had1 nothing, but most of them had much less than nothing: that is, they were deeply in debt to the company's stores. Whether the miners themselves are right or are n<ot right, their idea is this: that this little work and cutting off of credit was all a means to an end, a means of forcing the men to accept the ten per cent reduction in wages proposed by the company for the 1925 rate. I can quite realize how the very beautiful province of Nova Scotia, with all the fine hospitality and fellowship of the people in that province, resents the amount of

The Budget-Miss Macphail
unfavourable publicity that is being given to it. Everyone who has talked to people from Nova Scotia knows how tremendously proud they axe of Nova Scotia, and so I understand and sympathize with their feeling of resentment that so much is being said about the trouble there. Still, Nova Scotians as such are not to blame for this condition, because this company is not a Nova Scotian concern, but it has the ambitious title of the British Empire Steel Corporation. It is far outside the bounds of the province. Many of the directors live abroad, some in England and they are entirely absentee. Three of them sit in the Senate.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hard on the company.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Tremendously hard on the company. I went by train to Sydney and of course one cannot go any further than Sydney by train. Then I took a street car and went to Glace Bay. It took an hour and ten minutes to get there. I was accompanied by the mayor of Glace Bay and the representative of the Great War Veterans' Association. When I got there I tried to be fair. I am sure some hon. members will find it hard to believe that. I visited some of the representative places. I visited the Young Men's Christian Association, which is the central relief station. I visited some of the sub-stations of New Aberdeen, and other places. They have funny names down there. They call one place the Hub, and another the Table 'land, these are different suburbs. I visited the headquarters of the United1 Mine Workers. I went through the hospitals accompanied by one of the 'leading surgeons there. I visited all the rooms of the school, and went through the school with the truant officer, a gentleman who had held the position of truant officer for a long time and had been a teacher before that. I met at least two . thousand miners at a mass meeting in the Savoy theatre in Glace Bay. I read in a paper to-day the statement that I had said, that if I lived in Glace Bay I would always eat at the Savoy theatre. That was a funny thing. I did not see anything to eat there, but that is where the mass meeting was held. I talked to preachers, teachers, nurses, and miners, every one I met there. I met the wives of doctors, and all the friends of people that one meets in such a centre. I met the moderates and the reds, and by the time I had spent two daj'S in Glace Bay nobody looked red to me. I think if I lived there long I would be a lot redder than anything I saw. The schools did not show the amount
of hardship that the hospitals and the homes and the relief stations showed. I took this to mean that the people were exceedingly anxious to keep their children in school and to put their best foot forward. They put on whatever clothes they could wear and whatever boots would fit, and the children were sent to school in that way. The British Canadian Co-operative Company has been doing a really excellent work in supplying a nice dish of warm soup for the children at noon, knowing that the children are not getting sufficient food at home, and they want to keep them in good health and mental condition, so that they can continue their studies undisturbed by the strike that is now on.
I do not want to exaggerate nor to overpaint the picture. I would much rather understate than overstate the conditions, because hon. members will get tired of it. Hon. members will think it cannot possibly be true. If any of my hon. friends take that view, I have only one thing to say-go and see. It is quite noticeable that people who say there is no hardship are not on the ground, they are at a comfortable distance from it. I believe if anybody, whether director of that company or a shareholder, or a member of this government, even the member for Cape Breton South and Richmond (Mr. Carroll); will go to that district and stay there for a week or two, he will come to the conclusion that very real distress and human misery is found in those colliery towns. If anyone wants to spend an Easter recess in the interest of humanity, let him go and spend it-and I shall not be afraid of what he will find in contradiction of my remarks -in Glace Bay, Sydney Mines, Mine No. 6 or any of the colliery towns in that district. I saw some cars there and we went in one of them, a Ford sedan that succeeded in getting through the mud. It spluttered and stuttered but it got through. Four of us went in it-the little woman I spoke of before, the truant officer, a Great War Veteran official and the man who drove the car, who, they told me was a red, and myself. He was an exceedingly modest, pleasant fellow and I do not know Whether he was red or not. The first place we went to was a house of the two-family type-two families living in a nonpainted wooden house. The first door we went to, we were kindly invited in. There were five children in that home with the mother and father making seven. There were two bedrooms, a little sitting room with nothing in it, and a kitchen. The kitchen was small and had the usual kitchen furniture, two Chairs, a

The Budget-Miss Macphail
taible and a stove. It had never been a home for at least twenty years. If it ever had been a house that could have been made into a home, that was a long time ago. It was a most dilapidated place. There had been decorations on the wall once, but they were not intact. I went into the bed rooms. I saw the bed clothing, and1 you would hardly believe it, but there was just one blanket and one quilt on one bed, which clothing, as the woman told us and as the truant officer had told us the day before, came from the relief station, and on the other bed, there was just a quilt. That was all. They were at their meal when we went in. They bad been late in getting to the relief station, and as the demand is greater than the supply, they were only able to get a meal of bread, potatoes and milk, and that was a good deal better than nothing.
In the next home we visited' there was a family of four including two children, one of whom was at school.~ This was a tidy looking place. The house was not in good shape, but it was as clean as it could be under prevailing circumstances. One child was in bed quite sick, and it had not eaten anything for a week. It did not like eating the food that was placed before it. I do not know whether it was dangerously sick or not. I fancy it was not dangerously sick, but it was miserably sick. I can give the names and addresses of any of these people if anyone wants me to do so.
The next house was that of a returned soldier with six children, five boys and one girl. This was all in the newspapers. His house was not a company house, but it was a very poor house for which they paid twenty dollars a month. It was such a poor house that they were using only the downstairs, because the roof leaked and the plaster was falling off, so that the father and mother thought it was not safe for the children to be upstairs. The upstairs was not finished; it was just one room. Downstairs, there was the kitchen and one bedroom, in which the eight people, the mother, the father and the six children slept. The baby was four months old and the next one two and a half years who had never walked. The mother told me-and I am saying just what she told me-that the child was normal when born, but was now suffering from rickets and was not in good health. It never walked and it had spindly legs, like a thumb, not like the legs that a child of two and a half years should have. By the way, the place I have just finished telling about was on the edge of the sea, only a few yards from the wholesome sea that is at our
IMiss Macphail.]
eastern gate, as we read when we come into the entrance to this building.
The next place we visited was in New Aberdeen, the home of the widow and family of a veteran. The father had been killed overseas. There were six children, one under sixteen years of age and the mother did not get a pension for him. There was another one about twenty years Old who was married to a girl, both of them children to look at. They had two children and she was an expectant mother. The mother of the young man told me that she did not think it was too much to say that they bad had only one solid year's work in five. That may be overstating the fact, but that is exactly what she said. She looked around at us, so helplessly. Any woman with a heart at all would feel like striving to do something. She turned around and said: "What is wrong? What is the matter? We used to be able to work and have very good times." She was a miner's wife, who had been bom and raised in a mining town; she knew absolutely nothing else; but compared with her past experiences, what they were going through now she considered terrible. To me it would be unbearable, but to her i't did not seem as bad as that. These places were not chosen for me, because many times when they would want to go into one house, I would want to go into another and I went into the one I wanted to go into.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I see the joke. I did go into the houses I wanted to go into. We passed some fairly good-looking houses up towards the business section of Glace Bay that were not on the hunger line. That is certainly quite true. The next place we visited there was a man, his wife and two children. The place Was very clean and small, possibly the neatest place we were in. The clothing was clean; the whole house was clean. When we came out, the -truant officer said to the representative of the Great War Veterans' Association and myself: "I gave that man the clothes he is wearing" and the representative of the Great War Veterans' Association said: "Do you call them clothes?" That is about what one would say. He had on a red sweater that did not have any sleeves below the elbows. Still it was a sweater. I have worn one that was as bad, but I have had another. The hard part of it is that that was the only one he had. The wife was wearing a clean calico dress, which was ail she had. There was nothing back of that. A little child that she told me was seven, but that did not look over four, was wearing a coat, a very decent

The Budget-Miss Macphail
old coat, but no dress, and a pair of stockings that the mother had made out of cloth. She was warm inside, but she could not go outside. That is an actual condition.
I have some of these men's pay sheets. People wonder why they did not get out. They ask: What do they stay for? I wondered that too. This man worked four days, earning $14.80, but the check-off comes in: Rent, $2.14; coal, $1; attorney for his back store bill, that is for how much he is indebted at the store, S2; U.M.W., SI; relief association, 30 cents, church 40 cents, hospital 25 cents; and he had left $6.51 for a week's work.
This is what they call a bobtail. I was at relief store No. 2 and I aslked a group of very fine Scotchmen who were there if they could give me some bobtailed pay sheets. They said that was one of the things they were plentifully supplied with. This is one that I was given. This man worked two days, earning $7.40. Rent was $2.88; coal, $2.30, attorney for his back store bill, $1.02; hospital $1.20. There was nothing left. This is another one, and I will not go over the items. In this case the man worked three days and had $5.02 left. In another case the man worked two days and had $1.61 left. In another case the man worked three days and had $2.79 left. These are all from the same man. The man told me he would be glad to go away and he would be delighted to get work. He would walk out if he 'could not get out any other way. ' He had no money to pay train fare. But he said: "If the company knows that I have left them and am dissatisfied with conditions and possibly a publicity agent against them, my wife and children will be turned out of the company's house," because it is a company's house he is in. He said: "I am hopelessly in debt. I once just got out of it." He told me how he once owed $143 to the company's store and had just got out of that debt when cessation of work occurred again.
It will be seen therefore that these people are actually fettered as securely as though the links of the chain that bound them were visible. Let me take another family. These people came originally from Newfoundland, the family comprising the man and his wife and two children. The woman had been in hospital for a long time suffering from tuberculosis, as I learned from Dr. Macdonald- and when I say Macdonald you will understand that it might just as likely be McLean or McLaughlin or McNeill, for these are the prevalent names. He told me that this man was unable to support his wife in the private ward of any of the hospitals and they could not take the risk of keeping her in any of
the public wards. After awhile she was able to walk around and her case was really arrested. But she was instructed to procure eggs and milk and to take lots of fresh air, and in the endeavour to get the eggs they found it necessary to keep hens in the back kitchen. These people told us further that they were doing their very best to get milk and we were astonished to find that they were paying 10 cents a pint. So surprised were we at this that we took the trouble to have the statement verified and we discovered on inquiry that she was really paying 10 cents a pint for milk which was an absolute necessity in her case. And here is one feature of this case from which we simply cannot turn away our eyes: these four people, man and wife and two children, were actually obliged to sleep in one three-quarter bed, although as I have said the woman was suffering from tuberculosis.
I was in another home where the 9 p.m. inmates had not so far accepted relief-and all those whom I have cited were living off the relief stations. But these particular people, whose name is dear to me, a family of five, were suffering severely. The man is an electrician by trade and of course was out of work, but they had not yet accepted any relief. I had a conversation with the woman, who told me that although they had so far refused to take any help it would not be long before they would be obliged to do so. Let us remember that these people are haughtily proud, as I learned from one man when he drew himself up to his full height, blowing out his chest as politicians do. He said, "My name is Macdonald and I will never ask for relief". And that represents the spirit of the people. These people are not craving relief and they resent others sticking their noses into their houses; but they resent more haughtily the condition that makes that necessary. To convince the House that I am not making this up out of my head, I may say that I copied from the list of sub-station No. 2 in New Aberdeen, one of the worst districts where some 228 families are being fed, the names of one family numbering seven, as well as others. Some of these names I copied are, McNeill, McMillan, McDonald, McKinnon McIntyre and Munroe. This is the order in which I found them. I had a pleasant chat with two women at the relief station, one of whom although not an old woman in years was quite old in appearance. And that is the tragedy of womanhood there. She told me that her husband had had no steady work for a year and a half and although they were

The Budget-Miss Macphail
trying to do as well as they possibly could they could not help running into debt. There were seven children in the family, of ages ranging from ten months, to sixteen years, a few of them being at school. That woman came to the station in an old sweater and skirt, without any shoes, and with a very bad blister on her heel as a result of having to wear old rubbers. How anyone could keep rubbers on in Glace Bay without strapping them on is more than I can tell. There were no number fives to fit her at the station and she was asked to come back the next day. Her name too was McDonald-I will not give her Christian name to distinguish her from the other McDonalds. And mark you, Mr. Speaker, our own neighbours in the province of Ontario are called by these very names; to hear them one would imagine one was in Priceville or Glengarry. Another woman named McGillivray had three children who could not attend school, having no shoes; it was so wet in Glace Bay, as it is everywhere at this time of year but particularly there, that they were bound to stay at borne. I took her name and address for I intend to have some relief sent to this family and the one I mentioned a moment ago. This woman whispered in my ear an admonition not to forget herself and her husband because they were simply out of clothes. They had provided for the children rather than for themselves and they had positively reached the limit beyond which it was impossible for them to go. One could not help being struck by the fact that children of four years and under showed the miserable condition they were in. The children over that age are healthy but under that many of them, in the hospitals, in the junior rooms of the schools and on the streets as well, show plainly the malnutrition from which they have been suffering.
