speechtext: I want you to tell the truth.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have great regard for the truth, but these children I saw in the primary rooms would be only two and three years of age when the hard times struck them three or four years ago, and they had been under-

nourished for the last two or three years. I do not say of course that this is true of all the children there but the fact is that the hospitals are filled with such cases as I 'have described. And I want to say in passing that the hospitals are excellent institutions. I went through St. Joseph's and the General hospital and they were exceedingly sanitary and well kept. The matron who showed me through the General hospital and the sister with whom I went through St. Joseph's are fine types of women. I did see little babes particularly that were quite unhealthy looking as the doctors and nurses informed me. I took their word for , it, for I suppose a casual visitor would not be able to tell that there was anything organically wrong with them, from a passing visit. And they were all suffering from more or less similar conditions-ulcers, ricketts and all sorts of anaemic disorders; and there was one little baby with a paralyzed face, an infant about three days old. This of course was something that might be found anywhere else, and I was glad when the sister told me that the little thing would soon be going on. In the hospitals I noticed that all the doctors and their wives as well as the nurses and everyone connected with these institutions were very much concerned over the situation, because the hospitals depend upon the miners who contribute about 60 or 70 per cent of their upkeep. As a matter of fact, the miners are the population and they keep the hospitals and everything else going. One doctor who accompanied me on my visit of inspection expressed himself in no uncertain terms, and not as mildly as I am repeating them to-night, with regard to people who through the press and in their public utterances would Itead Canadians generally to believe that no distress existed down there. He told me that a week ago yesterday he was called to see a patient in a home where he found a family of eight, six children with their parents, in absolute destitution and entirely without shoes. He went to the relief station and obtained three pairs and out of his own money he bought five pairs at stores in Glace Bay.
The relief organization now existing there really grew out of a temporary and voluntary relief group of seven people, among them a very noble Jewish woman and a reverend gentleman, Mr. McAvoy, the wife of the mayor, and the little deaf woman who showed me about-the others I do not know; those were four of the original seven. They started this relief organization before the cessation of work three weeks ago because they knew there were children who could not go to school as they were not getting enough

The Budget-Miss Macphail
to eat, and there were adults in the same unfortunate position, so these seven persons busied themselves in gathering up from those who had to give it to those who had not. You see, the public opinion of Glace Bay, in fact the public opinion of the whole of Nova Scotia for the first time is supporting the miners. I am sure those who are familiar with Nova Scotia will admit that public opinion to-day is very much stronger on the side of the miners than it has ever been. It is becoming apparent to all who live in the colliery districts that their living is being sucked away by this process of strangulation of the miners. And so you find the whole middle class-I suppose you would call them professional people; I do not know whether in Canada we have lower, middle and higher classes, or not. I am not quite clear as to that-but at least doctors, merchants, ministers and their wives, have thrown themselves without reserve into this relief work. I saw in to-day's papers, and have no doubt other members also noticed the paragraph, that Mrs. Macpherson, the Salvation Army woman who has worked there from the first, says that the schools are likely to be closed because the salaries of the teachers cannot be paid. I now recall that when we visited one of the schools there the principal told me that they had not got their salary for last month. Although she said it in a joking way, it shows how dependent everybody is on the miners.
I want to make it clear for the sake of the real workers, I mean the miners themselves, that it was on the advice of these noble professional people who have interested themselves in their condition, that they turned down the gift of S5,000 sent to them by Russia. I said outside the House of Commons, and I want to say it here, that I think it is a very dubious compliment to Canadian intelligence that the miners of Nova Scotia and those who are working with them thought it necessary to turn down such a substantial gift in order that those people and their wants might remain respectable in our eyes. We are indeed a smug, self-righteous people.
You can imagine how chained these people feel. Surely we can get something of their sense of not 'being aible to get out of a hideous situation when we find that they cannot even get representation in parliament because their constituency is pocketed in a larger one which they cannot influence-or at least by reason of the methods employed in elections they cannot influence it. I am sure this House, I am sure members of the government, and I am sure the members who
sit for those constituencies have no idea how deep the resentment is, how intense it is, and how quiet it is. These people are not broken; do not ever think that. They feel that they have not got justice anywhere. Whether they are right or wrong I am not saying, but that is their feeling, and1 after all it is this kind of feeling that makes such a situation as exists there now a very dangerous one.
I want to describe the town so you will know how I felt when night came on. Up town are electric lights and! a sewage system, there are some paved streets and sidewalks, there is the Savoy theatre and there are some stores and rum shops-these are closed now. That is, there is a town there. But when you go back where the great majority of the people live there are no electric lights, there are no sewers, only open gutters flowing on each side of the road; there are a few houses where there is a way of getting water in, but for [DOT] the most part there are absolutely no sanitary conveniences at all. Just now in the springtime it is a bog hole, and when night comes, whether in the springtime or not, unless there is good moonlight the place is plunged in absolute darkness. After we had seem all this, after I had seen these women whom I have described, and after I had visited the hospital and met the relief workers and eaten my lunch in the relief headquarters, I said, "Is there anybody really red in this locality, red, red, red, the redder the better?" And they said there was one man. You know his name, it has been bandied about from time to time-J. B. Maclachlan. Then I said, "Take me to J. B. Maclachlan; I should like to see him." We went to the Labour Herald office. You know it prints wild things-and we too would print just as wild things if we suffered what they have suffered. I said^and I repeat it now, for you cannot arrest me- I said, "What is the worst thing Maclachlan ever said?" One man replied, "The worst thing I ever heard him say was 'To hell with them.' " I said I will add to it, "and make it snappy." You know that old joke about "sedition". Really it would be just as well if we never again charged a man with sedition in Canada. Do you know who Mac-lachlan reminded me of? Well, you would be surprised-J. J. Morrison; and I doubt if I can pay either of them a higher compliment than to compare them one with the other. Why, he has a beautiful home life. He is endeavouring to break the bonds, he is endeavouring to save a little money to buy a plot of ground and a home, he is endeavouring to get some culture. He has a beautiful family, a rosy-cheeked wife with a rolling

The Budget-Miss Macphail
Scotch tongue. And he is a man who has always stood for good citizenship. When I think of some of the things said by those who call themselves "good" citizens, I wonder really where we are going. Of course, these men say wild things. Naturally they do. They say awful things. But no one could blame them. Anyone who went to the same place and lived through the same conditions would,
I am sure, say the very same awful things. And I want to make this clear, because I think members of parliament are human- that means I have great faith in them-I believe they are. Mr. Maclachlan told me this story, which he did not intend 1 should repeat in parliament, and I am sure he will be horrified to read it. He told me that years ago, the very first time he ever came to Ottawa to negotiate between the miners and the company-just about the beginning,
I suppose, of this Besco concern, I cannot say whether it was before this or not-but at least, it was some years ago, when the company's representatives and the miners' representatives entered the Chateau Laurier-he had forgotten its name and I had to tell him-when the}7 sat down in the rotunda and looked at the luxury around them, he said, "I wanted to say something nasty, the nastiest thing I could think of, and I turned to the company's men and remarked, 'If you could bring the miners of the colliery district of Cape Breton into this place, you would not settle this wage dispute as you intend to settle it, and as you will.' " I appreciated that statement of his. Do you know, I am often struck by the fact that people who live at places like the Chateau Laurier pass the bill down, and the peopie who pay for it are never there? You see, my sympathy is very deep for these people, because they are primary producers, and their problems are just our problems only possibly in a more aggravated form.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And because they are
mostly Scotch.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, I sympathize with them also because they are mostly Scotch. Other people -corroborated this very story. One man, not Maclachlan, but a very moderate man, one whom the government would do well to encourage, said, "When some of our men went down to Truro last year to the annual convention, for days after they came back they could not talk about anything but the beauty of Truro." They said, "We did not know that such towns, with such homes for ordinary working people, existed." These are the facts. It seems almost ridiculous to think it could be true that anybody had not travelled that far away from

home in this advanced day of civilization. One woman told me she had not been out of Glace Bay for twelve years because she never felt she could afford the money that would take her over to Sydney and back-seventy-five cents. On the other hand, I do not want to suggest for a moment that miners, when they have money, are not good spenders; I rather think they are. I think that when they were making money they possibly spent it freely. Indeed, I am sure they must do so in order to forget the barrenness and dreariness of their lives as much as they can. It would be but natural to think that, when you consider how utterly lacking in beauty this place is. I never saw anything so devoid of beauty as Glace Bay in the spring. I wish you could see it-those bogs for roadways, with open gutters at the sides of them; those squatty, painted houses, row on row; the bleak winds of the sea; no vegetation, no trees. I can quite believe that when these people get money they buy a car; they go to the Savoy theatre twice a week or as often as their funds w7ill allow. They cannot make their homes comfortable; they are in the grasp of circumstances too great for them. And just a quarter of a mile away, up town, there are at least paved streets, bright lights, rum shops and the Savoy^do you wonder, then, that they flock there, where they can get at least what they think is some little pleasure?
It would seem to me that the best safeguard of citizenship w'ould be to strive to make the miners help themselves; not to try to break their union, but rather to encourage them sanely to get themselves on such a basis that their standard of living will be equal to the standard of living of other Canadians. I thought Mr. McLeod, president of the United Mine Workers for District No. 26, an exceedingly sane man. He is a moderate; in fact, they accuse him of being too moderate. At least he is anxious for the best things for the men. He knows that if there is any outbreak on the part of the men, it will be the men, not the company, who will suffer; he knows that there will be men thrown into prison, as was done before, and that they will come out with broken, embittered lives, the very worst influences in the community. So he is striving to teach the people and to get them to see that if they could once get out of the clutches of the company's stores and into a co-operative store of their own; if they could only get houses which they partly owned and could continue to pay for and try to beautify; if they would strive to work together through their unions for the good of all-that that is the way out, not in raid-'

The Budget-Miss Macphail
mg stores, breaking windows, and that sort of thing. His influence is all for the good. This government, the company, or anybody else concerned in the affair, ought to be glad to encourage the continuance of a union under the leadership of Mr. McLeod.
I would not like the company to think that if they break the union which exists now they will have broken everything. What I think will happen-and many people have voiced this opinion to me-if the union is broken, as has been done among the steel workers in Sydney, is this: a much more radical organization will take the place of the union, an organization that possibly even we would not want to see.
I could mot help but be struck by the tragedy of womanhood in that place; because to be a woman in a colliery district is a tragedy. Their youth is brief; there are many children; there is poverty, age coming quickly; dependency, and death. I do not know how they have kept the little spark of life that their faces still show: there were some young men and some young women who were hotly resentful of the conditions and not afraid to voice their feelings in the matter. But for the most part, especially if they had many children, their attitude was subdued, pathetic -I can think of no other words that so well describe it.
I would like to ask this government, have they an immigration policy? Or is it true that it is people like Besco and the railways and organizations of that kind that have an immigration policy? We find that Besco has been bringing in immigrants, even during the worst times; they have agents stationed all over the world who are bringing in immigrants, dumping them down where there is no work for them and doing absolutely nothing for them after they get them here. Do you wonder that labour resents that sort of thing? Do you wonder that all the resentment that these years have built up is directed against that company? No, you cannot wonder that they are resentful. Much money is spent to bring immigrants to Canada. These Scotc'h-Canadians-with the exception of some Scotch-Canadians-are the very best citizens we have; yet the women who give us these good citizens are not cared for; they are ldft to shift for themselves. What about them? This is the attitude that seems to have been taken by all governments, provincial and federal up to date.
It did not seem to be difficult for the company to get protection on coal, but the government gives no assurance that that protection is to go down to the worker.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Was that the thirteen? It looks to me as though the very great distress of the miners of Cape Breton to-day has been used by the company for their own protection. While the papers of the east heralded the announcement in the budget as a great thing, I did not find the miners thinking that-and I was in the town the day the budget came out; they felt entirely hopeless regarding anything that protection could do for them. They knew where that protection would go, from past experience.
When you think of it all-and I have almost finished with this tale of woe-when you think of it all, do you wonder that these miners have come to the conclusion that industry is heartless, that the courts are unjust, that all politicians are rascals? Do you wonder?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what they think.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hope they did not think that of you.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not a politician. One cannot but be surprised at the attitude of the Nova Scotia government, one of continued indifference, apparently, to a very grave situation, a situation which at any moment may break out into something really terrible; because we are only depending for relief on the generosity of Canadian citizens. It is hard to explain the attitude of the Nova Scotia government unless it be that they are afraid of this industrial monster; that they are more anxious to court its smile than they are to save to happiness and good citizenship many thousands of our fellow Canadians. One can almost imagine them asking themselves: What to them is environment for miners that will produce strong men, happy women, and healthy children; what to them the final destiny of our country, so long as power remains intact? Of course the government here can say there is a technical difficulty and that that prevents them from doing anything. They cannot send relief; they cannot inquire into this thing, because the Nova Scotia government, which lies closer to the miners, has done nothing. But I have seen this government find its way round technicalities before to-day. If the heart of the government was really anxious to do something 'to relieve the great distress among the people in the island of Cape Breton, they would find a way round the technical snag.
Really to my mind the whole cause of it all is this: We have put the commercial value
The Budget-Mr. Dickie

of making dollars and cents above the making of human life and creating comfortable conditions of living. I cannot think it is due to anything else. Our citizens will go on I am sure doing what they can to supply the needs of Cape Breton. Down there they are looking with great gratitude, almost with amazed gratitude at the wonderful things the city of Ottawa has been doing for them. Other places are following suit, and I am sure that the desired relief will come pouring in. But it is a peculiar situation that the governments concerned-the local government and the federal government-cannot come to the assistance of these people; that they can do nothing for the miners but leave it to private people to tax themselves to provide the necessary assistance.
I have nothing more to say. I leave the problem to the government. For it is a problem, and its solution, possibly, will demand something more than direct relief. It may be that there will have to be a genuine shaking up before long. I do not know whether that time is now or not, but I do know that when Canadian public opinion is aroused, and it is being aroused in this case, it is not going to stand any more fooling on the subject. I really feel sure of that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid that any words of mine may seem commonplace after the eloquent address by the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) to which we have just listened. However, I am going to put a few common sense arguments before the House in an endeavour to do something to alleviate the condition that prevails in Canada to-day. My remarks are going to be brief. The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton) and the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) in eloquent speeches have pretty well diagnosed the existing situation. It only remains for me to touch simply the high spots. These hon. members, with their actuarial minds and brains, have handled the problems before us in a much better manner than I can do. Suffice it to say that extricating the situation from the maze of clerical and arithmetical intricacies in which it is involved we find that in Canada to-day we are $100,000,000 poorer than we were a year ago. I think we will all admit that the liabilities of Canada are greater by $100,000,000 than they were at this time in 1924, a very serious state of affairs.
Now, what is the remedy? It seems to me that in discussing the tariff there is one vital phase that is lost sight of, and that is the necessity of keeping our money in Canada. I

remember in speaking before in the House on this subject but the point did not seem to be appreciated to the extent to which it should be. We are sending out of Canada every year $300,000,000 to our friends across the line. Three hundred millions from a population of nine millions of people means about $33 for every man, woman and child in Canada, how can we pay that huge amount and succeed? We must stem the outflow to some extent; we cannot do it entirely. After paying our interest debts to England we have a fair balance of trade of about $92,000,-
000.	We take that and we hand it over to our American friends, and our total contribution to them to-day amounts to hundreds of millions of dollars. WTe cannot succeed if we continue doing this, and the remedy for this state of .affairs, is, I consider, to keep our people from buying so much from the United States. We have to trade with these people; we know that they are good friends; they buy from us and we buy from them; but still it seems the acme of nonsense that for iron and other metalliferous and non-.metal.lic products we sent $265,000,000 to the United States last year. We also sent $78,000,000 for agricultural products, a total of $343,000,000. This sum that we sent to our neighbours across the line we could very well cut in two and thus save Canada a million odd dollars. The remedy is to import fewer goods. Last year we did not import quite as many as have been imported in years gone by. The reason was that we were not able to do so. Another reason was that many of our people are now living and working in the adjoining republic and are making their purchases there.
We talk of the hard times. It is pitiful to hear a tale such as has been told by .the hon. member for Southeast Grey. On the other hand we were assured by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock) that times were better in Canada than they were in the United States; that in the latter country there were 20,000,000 of people out of work. We were also told by the Prime Minister that the factory whistles were blowing at midnight throughout Canada. The factory whistles are not blowing at midnight in the town of Woodstock as instanced by the Prime Minister. The Bain Wagon Company had a little rush order on sleighs and they worked for a while at night but the factory whistles are not blowing there at night now. It has also been proved that they are not blowing at night in the case of the factory in Orangeville. What is the good of tiying to tell people that times are good in Canada. We would like if that was

The Budget-Mr. Dickie
the case, but times are not good in Canada, and they have not been good for some time. It is almost impossible to enlist capital in any industrial enterprise in Canada to-day because manufacturers are distracted by taxation, not knowing which way to turn. One reason is that the people have not the confidence in the government that they should have, although I am not going to emphasize very strongly that feature of the situation. We have our frightful railway problem, that "old man of the sea," bestriding us, and I do not know what the outcome of the situation is going to be. We must stop this drift to the country to the south if we are going to succeed. We are told that our people are coming back from the United States. In 1924 there were 41,000 returned but there were 161,000 that went, so that we cannot attach undue importance to any reported repatriation movement. Our people are still going to the United States where times are better and the opportunities are greater. It is just possible that in the adjoining republic, where they have had a period of uprecedented prosperity, things are now a little quiet, that they have passed the peak of the anticline. We in Canada have been wallowing in the trough of syncline; we have never got to the same stage as our neighbours as far as prosperity is concerned. In years gone by when they had prosperity on the American side it was sometimes reflected in Canada ; we had a certain degree of it here. When it was a case of our people leaving Canada and going to United States it lessened our population; and I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what would have been the experience in the case of our bread lines if a portion of our population had not gone? Instead of having thin bread lines we would have had bread battalions, and the burden would have been too great for Canada to bear. Strong virile men have been leaving this country and going to the United States instead of staying here and swelling the bread line. It is a great pity. I remember going back a few years ago into the county of Oxford through the country that I was familiar with as a boy. In those early days at every prominent four corners you could see strong, husky Canadians tossing the caber or indulging in other athletic exercises. Where are those men now? The government says that we must reduce the cost of living. In those days one could live for $2.50 a week. Living was as cheap in Canada as in any other country in the world. Those strong men to whom I refer have left the country but did they go to other countries where living is cheaper? Are they living in equatorial countries where bread fruit grows on the trees and 111
when the tide is out the table is spread? Not at all. Some of them went to the great west to Deadwood, Dakota, to Leadville, Colorado, and others again to the Yukon where ham and eggs cost a dollar or two a plate. They were not looking for cheap living. Cheap living is a fallacy in any country. You can always go some place and live cheaply. The thing is to have such a living that the agriculturist, the market gardener, the poultry man, the fruit man, the produce iman, and everybody else can succeed. It is impossible for a small farmer to succeed in the neighbourhood of, say a great city, if living is unduly cheap. It is the ability to purchase, not cheap living that we want. Daniel Webster once said:
A well-employed and prosperous community can buy and consume; an ill-employed community cannot do so. This is a solution of the matter. The whole science of political economy is not one half as important as this.
What we want is earning power. We want a chance for our people to earn money, and when they have earned money they are willing to pay decent prices. I have every sympathy for our friends the Progressives. Personally they are gentlemen, but I think, Sir, if they persist in the fallacy of free trade that prosperity for Canada is absolutely impossible. I do not think there is any chance for Canada being prosperous under such a policy.
An bon. MEMBER:	Cheer up.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I dio not need cheering up. I am cheerful. The only remedy for Canadians is to buy more in Canada, and the only way we can induce them to do that is to keep the people from buying across the line. I believe in an adequate protectionist policy that will make the people buy at home. If necessary in order to make them buy at home, I would not hesitate one moment to put our tariff wail one brick higher than the tariff wall of the country to the south of us. Why should we be guided by these people, they having a population of a hundred and ten million, and we a very small population? Why should we govern our action by their policy? Our small country requires much greater protection than the great country to the south of us.
I have very little sympathy with the talk of secession. We are Canadians, and I think if we buckle on our harness and put our backs to the south we can make this country one worth living in. We have wonderful potentialities. In the great Laurentian and pre-Cambrian plateau, we have the greatest potential region in the world to-day and the greatest possibility for gold1 mining. We have in the west our

The Budget-Mr. Dickie

wonderful forest resources not yet exhausted. We have wonderful potentialities, but we must have a spirit of compromise. No country can succeed if its industries do not succeed', and our industrial institutions cannot succeed in Canada without an adequate tariff. Our friends to the left of us here desire a good price for their wheat, and when wheat goes to two dollars a bushel every man, woman and child in the country is glad. Of course the cost of living goes a little bit higher because of the rise in the value of wheat, but we are glad that one part of the country is successful. However, when we ask them to stand a little tariff, and perhaps pay a little more for agricultural implements in order that thousands of people may be enabled to live in our industrial centres, they fall back upon the old cry of "Free trade, free trade." I say that free trade is the curse of England to-day. If it were not for a lot of economically silly old college professors with peculiar ideas they might have had protection in the Old Country. Why, Mr. Speaker, should we say that all the rest of the world is wrong and we are right-all except England-poor old England with a million and a half unemployed, using goods made in France, Belgium and Germany made by men who are working for cheaper wages than those paid in the Old Country? England wants protection and wants it badly, although no country in the world is better situated to succeed under a free trade policy than England.
I am going to worry the House a little with another question of which I am sorry to say no mention is made in the budget. I refer to the export of our raw material from Canada. Editorials have appeared in many of the papers in Canada with respect to this question. A pulpwood commission was appointed in 1923 and travelled through the country at an expense of 875,000 and collected a lot of useful information, which was well compiled. There were two practical men on the commission, and against whom or the other members I am not saying anything derogatory. Mr. Anstie, from British Columbia, vice-chairman of the commission whom I know well is quite heavily interested in timber, and it would be to his advantage to prevent saw logs leaving British Columbia. I know it to be a fact that the other gentleman, Mr. McLellan, from New Brunswick, is or was very largely interested in the export of pulpwood, and it would be to his interest that pulpwood be exported. This commission travelled! through the country listening to testimony in all parts of Canada,

but the evidence was absolutely one-sided. The commissiou compiled a fairly good report and made very sensible recommendations to the House of Commons. Wherever they went the people wjho were interested in exporting our forest products saw to it that their case was well presented by able lawyers. The general public was apathetic. I know that was the position in British Columbia. [DOT]I stated last year on the floor of the House and repeat to-day that although the evidence [DOT]of British Columbia was against the export of our raw forest products, if a plebiscite were taken I think seventy-five per cent of the people of British Columbia would vote to prevent our sawlogs being exported to the sawmills on the other side. The commission did a good work, and their findings were fairly reasonable, all things considered.
The investment in the pulp and paper industry of Canada in 1917 was 8187,000,000. [DOT]In 1923 we had 8417,000,000 invested, which shows the wonderful strides the industry has made. There were at that time 29,234 men on the payroll, the amount paid out being
837.243.000	annually. In 1924 we exported [DOT]1,444,093 cords of pulpwood, for which we received $14,322,714, and the manufactured value of a cord of pulpwood was $63.44. Had this 1,444,000 cords that we exported been manufactured in Canada it would have had a value of $91,651,313, less the amount received, $14,322,714, making a loss to Canada of $77,328,599. If pulpwood exports were [DOT]manufactured in Canada, this 1,444,000 cords [DOT]would justify an expenditure in a pulp and [DOT]paper plant of $125,000,000, and would mean the employment of approximately 10,000 men, with a payroll of $12,000,000 a year. That is what we are losing by shipping the pulpwood out of Oanada. In the year ending March 31, 1924, Canada exported in pulp and paper to the American side, $144,030,679.
When the question came up in the House a year ago the Prime Minister said he would not favour any duty or embargo on pulpwood that would interfere with the farmers or settlers who were taking wood off their wood lots. The farmers export sixty-five per cent of the total export according to the report of the commission. That would amount to 938 thousand cords. For this they receive $9,380,000 less freight charges. If this pulpwood had been manufactured in Canada the value would have been $59,469,000, less amount received, $9,380,000. Canada's loss would be $50,089,000. The farmer's average receipts per cord of pulpwood amounts to $6. For these
938.000	cords in 1924, the amount that the farmers and settlers received was $5,628,000

The Budget-Mr. Dickie
It must be borne in mind in connection with the commissioner's report that many bogus settlers take up land in the clay belt just for the sake of the timber. After the timber has been taken off or is depleted, they abandon the property. The report mentions these bogus settlers, but in the premises I am stating at the present time I am assuming they are all good, legitimate settlers. If they were compelled to sell in Canada, they might get 25 per cent less than they get on the American side. This is quite a substantial reduction, and supposing the market existed, the farmers loss would be $1,400,000. Therefore, Canada loses $50,000,000 in order that the settler or farmer should make $1,400,000. I defy anyone to contradict these figures.
The total exports of wood, wood products and paper to the United States in 1924 were $230,000,000. From this, one can realize what our adverse balance of trade with our neighbours to the south would be were it not for our exports of wood, wood products and paper. Still, we are recklessly depleting our forests and shipping our raw wood to our friends across the line instead of having them come into Canada and do the manufacturing here. It is not only wood that enters into the manufacture of pulp and paper. Many men are employed outside. Let us take the materials used in the pulp and paper mills in the Abitibi district. In 1923, a record was kept of the number of freight cars that passed in and out of the yards of the Abitibi Power and Paper Company at Iroquois Falls in -northern Ontario. The total was 30,801 cars, of which, 5,923 cars contained paper, 2,052 cars, coal; 6,169 cars, pulpwood; 148 cars, sulphur; 178 cars, limestone; 88 cars, alum; 24 cars, oil; the balance being empties. That shows the immense traffic that is furnished to our Canadian railways by these pulp and paper companies.
In British Columbia the logging exports in 1924 amounted to 240,000,000 feet B.M., and from government lands, licensed lands, 46,000,000 feet B.M. Sawlogs from licensed lands are not supposed to be exported from British Columbia, but the law is more honoured in the breach than in the observance. The reason is that, if there is a greater supply of logs than is required in the mills, because of conditions which exist there, the principal one being that our logs, if they lie in salt water too long, become infested with the toredo and are a loss, the privilege is accorded of shipping the surplus supply of logs across the line. That is just the same as if we had no barrier at all. We have enormous camps there under American capital with their railways extending 111*
into our forests, and as long as the British Columbia mills can secure all the logs they need, the balance is exported.
Last year we cut in British Columbia 2,550,000,000 B.M., twenty-five per cent greater than the cut of any previous year. In British Columbia, Washington, Oregon and California, it has been recognized that the last great stand of timber exists on the North American continent, and we are going through it as a reaper would go into a field at the present time. We still have a great deal of timber in British Columbia and should conserve it. We do not want to ship it to the American side and see our men following it. I am sorry to say that if you go, as I have had many times to go through these camps, you will find very many workmen who can scarcely speak our language. They are Russian Finns, Scandinavians, a splendid type of men who do our logging, but unfortunately, most of them are single and they are what we call a floating population. When wages and opportunities of employment are better in the United States, they go to the other side of the line. When they can get better wages in Canada, they come to our side. They are not the class of people we like to have, not because of any question of merit, but because they are a nomadic people. In British Columbia, I do not know whether our Anglo-Saxon people have been contaminated by jazz music and rotten Hollywood shows, but they do not take kindly to logging camps.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am dealing with the saw-log question now. A little later, I will suggest a remedy, and probably my hon. friend will agree with my suggestion. At the present time I am dealing with the appalling depletion of timber in the west. I remember distinctly the condition of affairs in Michigan in the early days. In those days I was privileged to go through a good deal of that country, being a log scaler. I remember standing in those virgin forests as a boy and thinking:	Well, here is timber for the
world for a thousand years to come. Wherever you looked there was a splendid stand of virgin timber. Ten years from that date they were importing sawlogs from the
The Budget-Mr. Dickie

Georgian bay to keep their mills going on the Saginaw river. They went through that forest as a reaper would go through a field of grain; The woods were filled with industrious, capable, cheerful men from the province of Quebec, men for whom I have a great admiration, whom I have envied, men always happy and industrious, with whom one had no trouble at all and who were quite satisfied if they were accorded fair treatment, I do not know where that race has gone now. We have but few of them in the west. Even in my time that section of Michigan has been entirely depleted of timber and they are importing lumber from British Columbia into Michigan every day. In Wisconsin, the same condition exists. In northern California, in the counties of Mendocino, Humboldt and Del Norte, where the red woods used to come down to the Pacific shores, the forests are shoved up the rivers into the mountains. The forests there are being depleted very rapidly. People will say that the forests will grow again. In Oregon it has been demonstrated that it takes fifty years to grow a tree one foot through, and that applies pretty well in all parts of the Pacific coast where growth is really prolific. If any hon. member cares to go out and count the rings on the cross section of a tree in the grounds adjacent he will easily be able to prove that what I am saying is correct. I will guarantee he will find fifty annular rings in the first foot and no more, but if you count them for two feet, you will find that there are 150 rings. That means that a tree two feet in diameter is 150 years of age. The larger the tree, the slower it grows, and consequently you have to figure on 150 years to get what we call a good British Columbia sawlog. People will say that the annual increment keeps up with the depletion and they use every argument they can in order to defeat any restriction being placed upon the export of sawlogs. In northern Ontario, and, I know, in British Columbia there are great areas of_ what we call mature forests. Trees, as with leaves, have their time to fall. They live only a certain length of time. I have walked through those silent aisles of the forests with great columns rearing themselves on all sides, and have seen dead tops in all directions, trees ripe and dying. There is no annual increment in mature forests but there is an annual decay. After the trees have become ripe, and once they have reared their crests heaven high, the trees begin to die and when they die there can be no increase in forest growth until after a fire or destruction.
TMr. Dickie.]
I come now to the question of hardwood logs. I am not very familiar with this question but with the permission of the House I shall read again from the Financial Post an extract which I quoted a year ago. I do not like reiteration but I have not seen the point disputed and the article I am about to read shows the necessity for some action.
The Ontario legislature will be asked to approve of legislation placing an embargo on the exportation of hardwood from the province. The measure is designed to force United States plants in Minnesota and Wisconsin to cross into Ontario to manufacture their products if they desire to use Ontario hardw'ood. The measure is similar to the pine embargo of some years ago. That measure resulted in many saw mills locating in the north. There are about 1,300 hardwood plants located in Wisconsin and Minnesota. Henry Ford entered the area and purchased practically all the available reserves. The estimate made to-day is that the end of seven years will see but 100 to 110 of these plants remaining because of the exhaustion of their supply of raw material. Realizing this there has been a rush into Algoma, United States concerns have eagerly sought control of the available limits on the Canadian side. It is understood that one American concern made a contract to ship 100 million feet of hardwood across lake Superior. This was to have gone to the Iron Mountain plant of Henry Ford. Ontario's reserves of hardwood are limited. The estimate is that the small area in which hardwood thrives contains 6,500 million feet. This includes the big forest reserve and runs north to the border of the clay-belt. In discussing the embargo, Hon. James Lyons, Ontario's Minister of Lands and Forests, pointed out that some years ago the numerous saw mills around Saginaw and Bay City, Michigan, were importing Canadian logs heavily. An embargo was placed on their exportation with the result that there is $75,000,000, invested in saw mills around the Soo to-day. The Canadian Pacific Railway line, Soo to Sudbury, is studded with them. He also points out that in 1900 there was an embargo in regard to pulp with the result that $190,000,000 are invested in the pulp plants of the province to-day.
The forestry department's statistics claim that there is in Canada of pulpwood 871,-
720,000	cords, 65 per cent being first class. Of' this, merchantable spruce and balsam amount to 580,000,000 cords. In Ontario, Quebec, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick there are 280,000,000 cords of which approximately 5,000,000 cords are cut annually. The forestry department estimates that cutting, fire, insects, winds and decay deplete the forests to the extent of 40,000,000 cords annually. In the last ten years it is reported that the spruce bud worm has destroyed 100,000,000 eords, and Mr. Sebrecht, a forest authority, puts it at 150,000,000.
Mr. Barnjum, rightly or wrongly, has been traduced all through the west, it being alleged that his motives in this matter are not unselfish. I have heard propaganda which has been inspired by people who were anxious to export our pulpwood and who declare that his actions are actuated by 6elfish considerations. They impute unworthy motives to him; but I
MARCH 31, 192o
The Budget-Mr. Dickie
know that he has spent a fortune in trying to impress upon the Canadian people the advisability of preventing the exportation of our forest products. Now, with regard to the growth of trees, in order to emphasize the facts I desire to quote from an article that comes from Nova Scotia:
"Most extravagant ideas exist as to the rate of growth of trees, observations of single trees growing in the open being taken as a basis to be translated into performance by whole acres of trees. The idea prevails that Nova Scotia spruce in the Nova Scotia climate is growing at an extraordinary rate. As a matter of fact, while it can be stated that the climate is most favourable to reproduction, i.e., to the establishment of young growth, the rate of growth of trees in the forest is not very different from the ordinary rate to be found in the New England States under similar conditions.
"Some 550 trees were analysed as to their rate of diameter growth, and a number of sample plots were measured to arrive at a conception of growth conditions. From these measurements it appears that to produce a spruce tree, 12 inches in diameter on the stump, may require from fifty years for the most favoured trees, to one hundred and seventy years for trees which had for a long time to compete for light with their neighbours. The unusually rapid-growth trees are, to be sure, found only occasionally; the much more usual rapid growers require eighty to ninety years to make the 12-inch diameter.
That shows how long we might expect to look for a new forest. I know mountain sides that were logged or burned forty-10 p.m. years ago in British Columbia where now there is little sign of any new forest of the Douglas fir type. Usually when a Douglas fir forest is destroyed it is re-seeded by hemlock or broad leaf trees. There are of course new growths of fir forests in different places where the conditions are ideal but as a general rule this does not occur. After severe fires, for some reason or other we get a growth in many instances of hemlock instead of fir. Anyone who has been through the southern Kootenay country, as the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King, Kootenay) has been, knows that around Eholt, Grand Forks, Greenwood and those places where there was formerly a good growth of pine there is now little but poplar. The remedy is to prevent the exportation of our raw material and otherwise to conserve it as much as possible.. But what I have read may not appear alarming unless I read something else- the recommendation in the concluding part of the report of the pulpwood commission:
So far as this commission is concerned, we have clearly pointed to the fact that some steps must most assuredly be taken whereby the annual drain on the spruce and balsam supplies of eastern Canada must be very greatly reduced. In some parts, this object may possibly be attained by the complete elimination of fire and insect losses; in other cases, it can only be attained by the elimination of such losses plus the reduction of the amount of spruce and balsam used either in local industries or in export. It has been
thoroughly pointed out that in the Maritime provinces the timber supply situation is extremely serious. On the theory of "ultimate exhaustion"-
And just a word on that phrase "ultimate exhaustion." Long before that time comes manufactories close down and all you find is
the wreckage of saw milling towns and camps.
On the theory of "ultimate exhaustion" there is only thirty-one years' supply of the pulp species. On the same basis, in Ontario and Quebec combined, in which provinces the pulpwood industry has its highest development, there is fifty-one years' supply.
This, however, does not take into consideration the losses by fire, insects and decay which are 40,000,000 cords every year. It is only a matter of a few years before the Maritime provinces and Quebec will be short of pulpwood, and I cannot see why we should persist in sending this raw material across the line. The argument is that the Americans will not come here but will	go	elsewhere for	their	pulp	andpaper if we put on an embargo. There may	be	something in	that;	but	thejare coming here rapidly now as we know We all know that United States investors have immense fortunes tied up in the pulp and paper industry of Canada. I have too great faith in the American people to think that they will adopt any policy of reprisal or retaliation. In fact there is no way in which they can retaliate in kind. And besides, what have we to thank them for in their treatment of us on tariff matters? They have said to us, "We don't want any of your canned goods, we don't want any of your western cattle, we don't want anything you manufacture; but we do want your raw products, your men and your money." That is exactly what is said to us, and we have been falling for it for yearn. The Fordney-MeCumber tariff says that plainly-a tariff characterized by one of the gentlemen to my left as having been brought about by the manufacturers of the United States. But as a matter of fact that tariff was put into effect just to suit a group of gentlemen similar to my admirable friends to the left, only living across the line. Our western farmers were sending their cattle and farm products into the States, and the American farmers said, "We don't want	any of	your competition." It
shows that business more than sentiment actuates the agricultural portion of our community, admirable as they may be.
As to the Americans retaliating or not coming over here to establish mills, I may say that up in the Soo region, on Manitoulin island, a big pulp mill is being constructed by the Fox River Company of Wisconsin. A few miles from where I live in British Columbia
The Budget-Mr. Dickie

we have what will be the last word in efficient saw mills, a mill that will cut a million feet every two days, and the company will employ four or five hundred men in the mill and about two hundred and fifty in the woods. They are going to cut logs into lumber there instead of sending them across the line. They are making a model town and will employ white labour, and some of the arguments used against saw mill owners do not apply to this 'company. Recently we saw in the newspapers the following article regarding the Canadian newsprint industry:
New York, March 6.-The newsprint industry is going to Canada, according to A. It. Graustein, president of the International Paper Company. Dispatches from Montreal yesterday announcing purchases of lands, mills and water power by the company, means nothing less than the transfer of a large part of the United States news print industry to the Dominion, Mr. Graustein said to-day.
When the new Canadian development is completed, he said, the International Paper Company would be able to produce 1,000 tons of newsprint per day in its mills in the Dominion. Outlining the plans of the company, Mr. Graustein said that if a contract with the newly organized Canadian International Paper Company, Limited, was ratified by stockholders, the Riordon and Gatineau properties in Quebec would be acquired.
"In order to preserve the position of the company and to insure its growth as a newsprint producer," he said, "it is necessary for us to develop in Canada. In the last twenty years the Canadian newsprint industry has come up from nothing to a point where it equals American production, showing unmistakably that the future of the industry is in Canada.
"We intend to build on the Gatineau river, near Ottawa, a big newsprint mill with at least the same capacity as our Three Rivers mill," he said.
Altogether the company intended to spend $27,000,000 for the Gatineau development, about $20,000,000 of which was for the mills, water powers and timber limits.
Another expression of the better class opinion which I claim prevails in the States is to be found in the Manufacturers' Record of New York. It says:
No country on earth can get rich shipping raw materials. Raw materials are simply the basis for the employment of labour, and labour creates the wealth which comes out of the use of raw materials. Wherever raw materials can be utilized at home, whether that be the United States or Canada, whether, so far as this country is concerned, it be the utilization in Alabama, for instance, of coal and ore, carrying the raw materials through to the finished product; whether it be in Louisiana in the utilization of gas or oils and sulphur, the Manufacturers' Record is heartily in sympathy with the policy of using these raw materials at home to as great an extent as possible. It does not believe that we can by legislation prevent the shipment of raw materials from one state to another. That would be unwise under our form of government. Canada has a perfect right to utilize its raw materials at home if it decides to do so. We have a perfect right to utilize our raw materials of all kinds at home for the production of manufactured goods, preferring to ship the finished product into Canada or other countries rather than send the raw materials abroad. It would be better, for instance, for this country if we could turn

all of our wheat into flour and ship the flour rather than the wheat, but that point has not yet been reached.
I am afraid I am tiring bon. members-
