speechtext: No, go ahead.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-but I have this subject very much at heart and I am trying to show where Canada can make millions of dollars. We know we have not illimitable timber resources. Every other country is beginning to conserve its forest wealth. Finland only allows such a limited amount of cutting as is compensated for by natural growth each year; Sweden the same way. They are reforesting, as is every other country in the world, they are all paying attention to their timber resources, while we are simply depleting our lands of all forest growth. The people who are opposed to any restrictions on the export of pulpwood have issued statements that the annual growth to-day is keeping up with the depletion of our forest resources. Let any man go up the Ottawa river, the Gatineau or anywhere else where timber is grown and see if he will assert that our forests are not being depleted. It is utter rot to say so. It is said only by men whose personal and selfish interests inspire them to make such unfounded statements. There is not an iota of argument against preventing our raw resources from going across the line. I have shown where we would save $70,000,000 or $80,000,000. And we need have no fear of lack of markets. The American newspaper men have already gone to Washington to try to head off what they know to be a sensible movement on our part, but they are getting little encouragement. They must come to Canada for their paper, and no doubt they will. As for any attempt at retaliation, they would be simply retaliating against themselves. In British Columbia it has been asserted, that 70 per cent of the timber lands alienated from the crown belong to American investors to-day. Those men are not going to see their investment hazarded by retaliatory measures, even though the minority of the people of the United States insist on reprisals; and, as I say, I have too much respect for them to think that they will ever attempt such a policy. I have seen editorials in other American papers corresponding with that which I have read from the Manufacturers' Record. Hon. members will remember that not very long ago President Coolidge made a notable speech with respect to preserving the forest wealth of his country. I remember when in Virginia, Louisiana and parts of Texas there were immense virgin forests; to-day they

The Budget-Mr. Dickie
are practically all gone. Many of these lumbermen have come to British Columbia to do what they did in their own country. The people of Virginia, Wisconsin, Michigan and Minnesota are all bewailing the reckless depletion of their forests.
It is perhaps useless for me to suggest a remedy; I do not favour an embargo, I do not think it is the right step to take, but I favour something pretty nearly the same. In British Columbia, if because of business stagnation, we had large quantities of logs in salt water, I should not like to see them destroyed. I would suggest that by order in council or some other way they should be allowed to be shipped out of the country. My idea would be that on Nos. 1 and 2 grades of fir, spruce, pine and cedar logs and on all hardwood logs an export duty should be imposed of $5 per thousand feet board measure; on all other logs, $2 per thousand feet; on all pulpwood exported by actual settlers and farmers from their land a duty of $250 per cord, and on all other pulpwood $5 per cord, to take effect January 1, 1927. I may be asked, why defer the imposition of these export duties to that date. I reply that Canada must act in a gentlemanly way. We have immense amounts of American capital invested in this country in our forest reserves, and I would give them a chance if they want to come over here and establish mills. They have millions of dollars invested on Vancouver island alone, and I do not wish to work any hardship on those gentlemen, so I would give them time. What I suggest is that in the interim the above duty shall apply on all raw forest products as above specified in excess of the 1924 exportation. That would prevent any attempt on the part of our friends to make a Roman holiday with our pulpwood; to come in and devastate our forests, piling the wood over on their side of the international line before 1927. In that way we would be protected.
With regard to the settler or the farmer taking wood from his wood lots, I submit that this country could pay those men to sit right at home and could still make $50,000,000 more than is being made to-day. We could make it up to them in some way. Possibly we should not say to the pulp and paper manufacturers, "You will have to pay so much a cord;" but there are ways of putting pressure on them and at the same time treating them fairly. Even though there should be no market at present for their pulpwood, I am sure the farmer-settler would make money by conserving it, by allowing it to grow for the time being. The value of timber will increase
by leaps and bounds in the next ten years; there is not the slightest doubt about it. This is the age of paper and pulp, and the farmers and settlers will make more by letting their timber stand than they will by cutting it. Up in the clay belt thousands of acres have been cut over by bogus settlers who have abandoned the property after cutting the pulpwood off and shipping it across the line.
I know that my hon. friends to my left are free traders just as strongly as I am in favour of adequate protection. But they must recognize that during the last two or three years many Canadian industries have gone out of business. It may be that times are improving just a little, but when you consider Canada's immense resources, its potentialities and the virility of its people, you will realize that we should go ahead by leaps and bounds rather than stand still or perhaps gain a little here and lose a little there. In this connection a matter was to-day brought to my attention which is worth mentioning. We have at Burrard inlet, Vancouver, a creosoting plant which represents a cash investment of $450,000. There is no duty on creosoted piling coming in from the American side. This company has a payroll of $30,000 a month, but the conditions now are such that they are seriously thinking of dismantling their plant. With a little protection they would be able to carry on; that payroll would continue and they would have a much better feeling toward British Columbia than they have at present. It is another case, very largely, of dumping from the American side. Over there they have enormous establishments; they sell to their own market, but they have a surplus lying in their booms and they use this when the opportunity offers itself, as in the case of a recent contract which came to my attention, in connection with the foundation of the dry dock at Prince Rupert. The Seattle creosoting plant underbid our own people; they offered a price much lower than it was possible for the British Columbia firm to quote for the supplying of creosoted piles. But the Northern Construction Company decided to pay more for creosoted piles from Vancouver than the price at which they could have got them from Seattle, and they were actuated by pure patriotism. Now, this is a condition which should not exist. The Americans simply dlough off their surplus piles to our city, at prices our people cannot meet, but when they have put the Canadian creosoting plant out of business then the price will go up, as has been the case in many other instances. So that if this industry is assisted something is done for Van-
The Budget-Mr. Dickie

couver, and the people will pay no more for creosoted piles than they are paying to-day.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) asked me if I would support him in connection with the subject matter of the resolution he has on the order paper dealing with naval protection on the Pacific coast. I do not know exactly what his viewpoint is; he had not concluded his argument when the discussion was adjourned. But it sounds well to me, as far as he has gone, and I would1 be very much in favour of the taking of some action along this line. The great naval headquarters at Esquimalt are in the district which I am humbly trying to represent, and I would like very much indeed to see a warship there, belonging to Canada or to Great Britain, upon which our young men- could be trained. My idea is that we should make a substantial contribution to the British admiralty and let them look after our ports. When those magnificent ships of the British navy were in our waters on both coasts last year, I in common with many Canadians felt a keen sense of humiliation. Here were those wonderful ships of war ready to protect us at any time, yet we were contributing hardly anything to the upkeep of the British navy. I know that we are in economic straits, but, Sir, as I said with respect to other matters, Canada should play the part of a gentleman, we should1 and we can afford to be a little more liberal than we are. Some people are saying to-day: Why should we want warships to protect our coasts with no war in sight. Sir, war is bound to come, we who live there know it must come-why should we require ships, when we are protected by the Monroe doctrine? Well, I have very little use for the Canadian who will wish to avail himself of the elastic provisions of the Monroe doctrine. The Monroe doctrine, as you know, is applied by the United States to suit their convenience. It is an admirable doctrine. Let me relate just a couple of incidents, Mr. Speaker, and I am through. Early in the war, as will be known to many, two German cruisers, the Nurem-burg and . the Scharnhorst, were in the waters of the northern Pacific. The people of Vancouver and Victoria were very much perturbed; some of them became panic stricken and left these cities, thinking that an attack might be made upon them. We weTe almost defenceless. We did have an old, obsolete boat and a couple of submarines- as to the submarines, when they submerged they never knew whether or not they would emerge again-but those who manned them were willing to live up to the best traditions

of British seamen. We knew, though, that they could have little effect on these large, up-to-date German cruisers. I remember talking to an American friend at that time, and he said:	"Would it not be very nice
if two or three of our vessels happened to pay Victoria a friendly visit at this time?" I said, "It certainly would." However, no American vessels paid us even a friendly visit. What we did see was a Japanese cruiser, stripped down to the decks, swarming with brown men, lying off our coast, ready to offer its protection.
The other instance I want to mention is this: When Dewey captured Manilla he was lying with his fleet in Manilla harbour. Admiral Diedrich came sailing in with a German fleet greater in strength than that of Admiral Dewey. Dewey pointed to a place for him to anchor, but Diedrich said he took his orders from His Majesty the Emperor of Germany and he chose his own anchorage. Diedrich then paid a visit to Admiral Chichester of the British fleet which was in the vicinity, and in the course of conversation with him he said: "What would be your attitude if I decided to attack the American ships?" Chichester said, " That is a secret between Admiral Dewey and myself." This is a matter of history; it is not hearsay. Diedrich knew what it meant. He left the British ship in a huff, and returned to his own vessel. The next morning when he came on deck he saw that during the night a British cruiser had steamed in and anchored between his warships and those of Admiral Dewey. As my American friends would say, " That was nice."

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I address myself to the budget, I should like, with the permission of the House, to conclude the remarks I was making on the resolution I introduced some weeks ago to the effect that " Canada should consider the question of the defence of our sea coasts and of our ocean borne lines of commerce ". I am sorry that this resolution will not come to a vote under the rules' of the House, but perhaps when the naval estimates are being discussed hon. members, especially those from British Columbia, will take an opportunity of expressing their views, and perhaps the Minister of National Defence will take the opportunity of expressing the policy of the government in that regard.
The House will recall that when I was speaking on this subject last I had shown or tried to show, that our coast, our property, and especially our shipping in British Columbia were entirely defenceless and that there

The Budget-Mr. Neill
was great need of defence, and I was examining what we had in the way of defence ourselves or what we would be likely to procure from outside sources. But before I go on with that I should like for one moment to go back to the question of the Disarmament conference and make a point that I omitted to make when I was talking on this question before. I suggest, Sir, that all the Disarmament conference did was to bring about an agreement among the nations of the world to do what they fully intended to do anyhow. In other words they made a bargain to do what the experience of the Great war had shown them was the most advisable thing to do; they made a solemn treaty to carry out what they had every intention of carrying out of themselves. For instance, the war had shown clearly that big dreadnoughts were not the most useful type of ship to use. Consequently the Disarmament conference made a solemn bargain to limit the size and number of dreadnoughts, or what they call capital phips, in future. It is true that they went further and made a limitation in regard to the size and armament of what they called auxiliary ships, otherwise cruisers, but I notice they were particularly careful not to limit the number of these boats; and while they did put a limit, in regard to the maximum size and tonnage, the limit was so high and the tonnage was so large that in reality it encouraged all the nations of the world to increase the size of their cruisers. For instance the average light cruiser, before this conference ran to seven or at the most eight thousand tons. Japan had building at that time four boats of seven thousand tons. The Disarmament conference decided that the maximum tonnage of cruisers was to be ten thousand tons and the limit of armament, I think, eight inch guns. So naturally the Japanese immediately redesigned the ships they had been building. They raised the limit of these cruisers to ten thousand tons and they increased the armament of those vessels so as to bring it just within the maximum laid down by the conference. Other nations followed the same course naturally for it would be foolish for them to have [DOT] smaller ships than their competitors. The result is that the Disarmament conference has actually increased the size and cost of light cruisers without in any way limiting the number of them that can be built. What will be known in the future as the "treaty" cruiser has arrived, and at the present moment the five signatories of that conference have laid down no less than thirty of these new cruisers. And that conference was only held
a couple of years ago! The treaty cruiser of the future will be a thirty-five knot ship with a battery of eight or more eight inch guns capable of developing a volume of fire of about thirty rounds a minute, and discharging a projectile weighing somewhere in the neighbourhood of two hundred and fifty pounds. In a word I think it might be justly said that the Disarmament conference, by virtue of its actual results, appears to have brought about a revival of armaments.
Now I shall describe the ships, or the means of defence, that we have on the Pacific coast. I said that we had a cruiser that was of very little value except for training purposes. We also have two mine sweepers. It is true that we have no mines, and no means of laying mines-no mine layers-and it is extremely unlikely that an enemy that might come and blow up or ransom any of our forte and towns would be likely to bring mines and lay them for us to sweep out,
[DOT] because that would be quite unnecessary. So that these mine sweepers are not of any particular value as regards that purpose. I admit, however, that they would be good for the pursuit of submarines.
Now I should like' to give two instances of what actually occurred in the war, and in making this statement I shall not be disclosing any secret, so as to give an idea of how acute the conditions were out there in the way of lack of defence. During the war a passenger boat was running up north to Alaska. It happened to have three funnels, rather an unusual thing, and the general cut of it in some ways rather suggested a light cruiser. That boat was taken off its regular merchant service-it had no armament-and was bolstered and painted up to make it look as much like a cruiser as possible and started out on the Pacific ocean in order to head off, if possible, German raiders and cruisers; and from a diary discovered on the body of one of the German officers killed in the battle off the Falkland islands it was actually discovered that on one occasion, at least, a German armed raider had fled from this boat believing it to be a British cruiser. That is one of the pretences we had to take refuge in.
Here is another instance:	The terminus
of the Pacific cable, which is a very important point during a war and still more important if the war happened to be on the Pacific, is at Bamfield on the west coast of Vancouver island. During the war this station was defended ostensibly by a handful of men with rifles. You can imagine what use such a force would have been against an armed raider. But it had the further pro-
The Budget-Mr. Neill

tection, or was supposed bo have, that the channel of five or six miles leading into Bam-field was suitably protected by mines; and every time a boat required to come in a pilot had to go out and guide the vessel through the mine field into safety and out again, the plain fact being, Mr. Speaker, that there never were any mines there at all; it was all a figment of the imagination calculated, or supposed-or we hoped it would-to mislead any German vessel from coming in to blow up the cable station. To put our whole dependence, in future wars, in artifices of that kind is surely not the part of reasonable and responsible men.
I have led up to the suggestion that we have no defence and that we need defence. Having no defence of our own there are only two outside sources by which we could attain it. The first that we would naturally turn to in an emergency is the British navy. In 1914 the British navy had 126 heavy and light cruisers. They could only spare a few of these for the Pacific, and we all know the enormous damage that was done by the Emden which, if I remember rightly, was not a cruiser at all but merely an armed merchantman, an armed raider. The fact that the Emden did an enormous amount of damage was not due to her armament, or anything of that kind but simply because there was no vessel bigger than herself able to get into contact with her. The record of that single boat, and the damage she did in the Pacific, ought to be enough to convert anybody to the idea that we out there ought to have some protection. I noticp that since I brought this matter up there was a. debate in the British House when the first Lord of the Admiralty pointed out what trouble the German sea raiders caused in the Great war and asked if it took seventy cruisers to round up these few German raiders, with almost the whole German fleet bottled up, what would be the prospect in a future war if British commerce were attacked by some other power.
There are two further matters I desire to mention. During the war a condition existed that will never exist in any war on the Pacific, and that is that the two great powers against us, Austria and Germany, practically had both their fleets bottled up in a port or in some channel, and the British fleet kept them there. Occasionally one would break away in the darkness and do a great deal of damage, but for the main part they were kept bottled up, and it was comparatively easy for the British fleet to concentrate their vessels and keep them there. But on the Pacific it would be impossible because the ports are all

open, and the British fleet would have to be much scattered, and their efficiency naturally very much reduced in that way.
I would point out also that owing to the Disarmament conference having induced Britain, to bring down her naval power, from a three to one to a one' to one basis, it means that in 1928 the British fleet of heavy and light cruisers, instead of being 136 will only be 57, and they will certainly be all needed to police the main trade routes of the Pacific if a war occurred on the Pacific. I think therefore, it is proved that we cannot hope that Britain can do any more than guard the main ocean routes, and it will be quite impossible for us to expect her to detach ships to guard what might be called the local coasts, of British Columbia, Australia, New Zealand and so on. These other dominions have realized the truth of that contention as we see in the fact that New Zealand has embarked on s policy of naval defence of her own shores so have Australia and South Africa. It is somewhat significant that the policy of the naval defence of South Africa is advocated by and going to be carried1 through under the leadership of Charles Hertzog, a man who, in the Great war only a few years ago, was in active rebellion against Britain, and it cannot be supposed that he is animated in this matter now by any great feeling of imperial enthusiasm. He is actuated by the conviction that if South Africa is not in a position to defend herself, she will be in a helpless condition.
So much for the idea that we can expect the British navy to protect the British Columbia coast or the Atlantic coast.
The other source from which we might hope to get some relief is the Monroe doctrine. That is a very much over-rated doctrine at the present time. I will quote the best definition of it that I have been able to obtain in one sentence, as given by President Adams. I will give you his interpretation of the Monroe doctrine, at the time of its inception. He says:
Considering the South Americans as independent nations, they themselves have the right to dispose of their condition. We have no right to dispose of them either alone or in conjunction with other nations. Neither have any other nations the right to dispose of-them without their consent.
That was the doctrine as it was formulated over a hundred years ago, but between that time and the present, conditions have changed entirely. The very evil which it was intended to prevent-that is the abuse or the coercion of the small American states by European countries-has been changed into a very much greater dread, not any more of the European

The Budget-Mr. Neill
powers but of the United States themselves. I should like to quote a sentence or two out of a very well written article on the Monroe doctrine by an American writer in an American journal, which cannot be supposed to be anti-American or pro-British. Here is what this writer says, talking about the diplomats of the United States:
To them the doctrine has become a diplomatic top bureau drawer, into which anything may be put and from which, after due pawing, anything may be produced.
I think that is a very good expression "after due pawing". The Monroe doctrine, from time to time,' has been used, added to and pared away, according as the emergency suggested and, in the interests of the United States only. Thus on one occasion it had an annex hitched on to it, .called the Doctrine of Paramount Interest, a lovely amendment, which allowed the United States to go into a foreign country -and do what they thought would be in the best interests, not of that country, but of the United States. Later on, when they encouraged a rebellion in a Central American republic, they invented another extension of the Monroe doctrine, and it took the form of the Doctrine of Preventive Intervention, by virtue of which the United States claimed, the right to intervene in the affairs of any of the Latin American states whenever in its opinion a state of affairs threatens to arise which may produce European intervention, which may in turn produce occupation of territory, which may ultimately produce annexation. If this is a doctrine of non-intervention, of protecting other states' national independence, then of course black is white. In spite of that language "we have no right", we find that, under the Monroe dioctrine, Texas was annexed against its will, to the United States, California, New Mexico, Porto Rico and Cuba, and there has been interference in Panama and Columbia. In other words, the modern interpretation of the Monroe doctrine is that no nation is to be coerced except by the United States. That is so openly feared that at a pan-American conference some years ago they endeavoured to get the United States to go back to the original meaning of the Monroe doctrine, but the United States would not do so, and the word " suzerainty " was quite openly used in reference to its relation to some of the smaller states; so that it is to this doctrine, with its cold-blooded indifference to the interests of any nation except the United. States that we are asked to appeal for protection and for defence in case of war. Moreover the doctrine does not apply to British possessions.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
How much does my hon.
friend say Canada should expend yearly to protect her shores?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will deal with that in a few moments. Moreover the Monroe doctrine does not apply to British possessions, and it only applies to where the independence of states is threatened. It does not forbid attacks on shipping or the collection of an enormous indemnity, or the collection of a war indemnity in the shape of large supplies of raw material for years to come, as was suggested would be one of the terms if the Germans had conquered in the late war. Then if we were driven by our defencelessness to ask for the application of the Monroe doctrine by the United States, what price would we pay for it? Scripture tells us that the lion and the lamb shall lie down together, but in that case the word " shall " is used. " Shall " suggests futurity. We do not know when that period will arrive, but history records no instance where the lion and the lamb have lain down together with any real satisfaction to the lamb. Take the record of Britain herself. There is no country in the world which has been so magnanimous in its treatment of vanquished nations, or so .generous in its rule over conquered natives. No nation can compare with Britain in that regard, and yet taking the record of Britain herself, where she has gone in very often with the most emphatic declaration that it was only temporary occupation for the good of the particular state, and with the fervently expressed intention of pulling out in a very short time, there are very few records of where she has ever pulled out again. It has drifted, perhaps, into a suzerainty; it has always become more or less permanent, I admit, very often, for the good of that nation or race, but still Britain has remained there, a permanent, unwelcome and uninvited guest. If we are driven by the misfortunes of our defenceless condition to seek the assistance of the United States under the Monroe doctrine, we are practically inviting that we become an appendage in some form or another of the United States. Some mention is made of the cost. The costliest way of all of defending ourselves in case of an attack would be by inviting the aid of the Monroe doctrine. It would be goodbye to our dreams of national existence. We would get requests which, by-and-by, would become demands, and by-and-by we would have absorption, or .control, or at least, that peculiar thing, known and already practised on other nations, as " preventive intervention."
The Budget-Mr. Neill

Moreover, it is quite possible in case of war that the United States would not be able to afford us any protection. A very able writer the other day made the prediction that, in case of war, if the Hawaiian islands were captured by an enemy, the whole coast of the north American continent would be at the mercy of the enemy. I submit the question is not: Can we afford to defend our coast? but, can we afford not to defend it? Take the case of a man owning a big business block and going to a mortgage company to ask for a big loan. The first question he would be asked would be: "Where is your title?" He could produce that. The second question would be: " Where is your insurance policy, and how much is it?" Supposing his reply was: "Well now, I want to tell you about that. I do not believe in fire. We are not going to have any more fires. I have joined an association to disown fires, and consequently I have not insured my building and do not propose to do so." Would that man get his loan? I do not think so. Are we in any better position as regards our national existence? Is naval defence not the premium on our national life insurance policy? I should like to ask this House, and through this House, the people of Canada: Can we afford to neglect to pay the premium on the policy of our national life insurance? I should like the House to think over that.
There are just two other points in this connection and I have done. One is that my advocacy of this suggestion will lead to militarism on a large scale. That is a very unfair unjust criticism, so unfair, unjust, untenable and indeed, inapplicable, that I think it can be put forward only by those who wish to confuse the issue, who want, not to face the issue, but to shut their eyes to the plain facts, and who think, by calling it militarism, they can dismiss the obvious situation I have presented. If I were arguing for or suggesting, even in a remote degree, a big fleet and army, they would be quite correct. But there is all the difference in the world between militarism and defence, between defence and defiance, between protection and aggression. Have we ever tried to stop crime by dismissing our police force? I do not think so. Will an absolutely helpless nation not invite the aggression of a truculent neighbour? I therefore repeat-and I wish to be so careful about this that it cannot be misrepresented that I have written it down-that what I am asking for is only-that the Parliament of Canada should consider and devis.e a policy for the defence of our shores and of our shipping, a policy within our means and to be carried

out as our financial condition allows us. Is that jingoism? Is that militarism? Is it not rather the sober, sane action of a business man who protects his business against loss by fire or his family against his own loss by sudden death?
There is just one other point in this connection. It has been suggested to me, not, I am glad to state, by any hon. member from the prairies, that the prairie members will take no interest in the consideration of a case of this kind. I do not believe that, and even putting the matter on the most material grounds, they are bound to take an interest in it because they are as much concerned ultimately as we are. The freedom Of Calgary and Winnipeg will be fought for, not at the gates of those cities, but on the Atlantic coast or on the Pacific coast. What will be their condition if they are cut off from the sea for three or four years? I know we in British Columbia would suffer first. Our coal mines which, heaven knows, are in a bad enough state now, would be the first to suffer. Our fishing industry would disappear. Our lumber industry would be at a standstill. But as the shipping disappeared the trouble would spread on to the prairies, and once they had no outlet for their grain, there would be a complete tie-up of the business conditions of Canada. It would paralyze every feature of the trade of Canada. Let us not forget, for we forget so easily, how nearly Great Britain was brought to her knees during the Great war, not by any lack of men or food or munitions, but by the threatened inability of being able to convey that food and those munitions to the men at the front.
I want to answer my hon. friend's question about the cost. I said at the beginning of my remarks the other day that I was particularly careful to define no detailed scheme for defence, because there are so many different ways, and to suggest one would only promote divergence of opinion upon the main issue. The particular line adopted would have to be decided by technical experts and largely governed by our financial ability at the moment. ,1 quite admit that, and I am suggesting that we go into no expensive scheme whatever. I will make this suggestion as to the cost. We have the skeleton of a very considerable standing army in Canada to-day. I should like to know, ini case of a sudden need for this army:	What nation could we use that
army against suddenly and quickly? There is only one nation that we could use it against in a hurry and that is the United States. The prospect or the possibility of war with the United States is so remote-and

The Budget-Mr. Neill
I hope it always will be remote-that it is quite unnecessary for us to consider it to-day and for many years to come. Therefore, if we have no need for a standing army, why have we one? The danger to Canada will come on our coasts long before there will be any need of an army. We spend roughly on the permanent force and on the active militia, if not on the active militia alone, somewhere in the neighbourhood of four million dollars a year. For instance, in the city of Ottawa, there are the skeletons, at least, of four different regiments, and I suppose the same is true in a greater or lesser degree throughout the whole of eastern Canada. You can make a soldier of sorts in six weeks; you can make a first class soldier, a fighting man, in six months; but it will take at least that many years to make a first class naval man. First of all, he has to be a seaman, and that is not done in a day or a month. Then he has to be a naval man, and this means a finely trained mechanic of a kind which you do not get in civilian life. The ordinary time for training a first class naval seaman would be six or eight years. Would it not be better to spend less on the militia, and what is saved on that might be spent on a nucleus, at least, of a scheme of naval defence? I am only throwing out a suggestion that would minimize the cost of any naval scheme that might be adopted.
I have spoken only about the Pacific coast because that is the one with which I am familiar. I am not ignoring the needs of the Atlantic coast, but I leave it to men more capable and better informed than I am to deal with that. I would suggest that the government consider, if not at this session, at the next one, the advisability of appointing a committee of a non-partisan character to study this question. Its importance can hardly be overestimated. I would conclude by summarizing in half a dozen sentences the arguments I have endeavoured to present tonight and the other evening:
1.	That our sea coasts are defenceless.
2.	That the need of defence is evident and urgent.
3.	That we cannot logically demand, nor can we reasonably expect the British navy to furnish that protection in case of war.
, 4. That it is highly undesirable that we should be driven to seek the protection of the Monroe doctrine.
5.	Let our motto be, aggression against none and defence against all.
Therefore, in the words of the resolution, I would shbmit that Canada should consider the question of the defence of our sea coasts
as well as of our ocean borne lines of commerce.. That, Mr Speaker, concludes this phase of my remarks.
